lessons.title: Deshalb trainiere ich: deshalb for results
lessons.goal: Connect a reason and a result with deshalb (position 1, verb next, then the subject) and talk about sport types.

grammar.point: Deshalb connects two main sentences and gives the result. It stands in position 1, so the verb comes right after it, then the subject: Ich bin müde. Deshalb gehe ich nach Hause. Full stop or comma before deshalb are both correct. With a modal verb or the Perfekt the second verb goes to the end. Weil sends the verb to the end, denn keeps the normal order.
grammar.oneLine: Ich will fit werden. Deshalb trainiere ich.

mistake.wrong: Ich bin müde, deshalb ich gehe nach Hause.
mistake.right: Ich bin müde, deshalb gehe ich nach Hause.
mistake.why: Deshalb takes position 1: the verb comes right after it, then the subject. The verb does not go to the end like after weil.

terms.meaning: that is why: it gives the result of what you said before
the first place in a sentence; the verb comes right after it
they give the reason; weil sends the verb to the end

cards.title: Before we start: from „weil“ to „deshalb“
cards.body: This chapter is about sport. Mira plays Volleyball at „SV Kanalufer“, Leon loves Handball, Ben starts running, Anna trains for the city run (der Stadtlauf) and Frau Weber swims. You already give reasons with weil. Today you learn the word for the result: deshalb.
steps: You already know: weil and denn for a reason (Ich trainiere, weil ich fit werden will) and zuerst / dann with the verb next.
New today: deshalb for a result (Ich will fit werden. Deshalb trainiere ich) and nine words for sport.
By the end you can: connect a reason and a result with deshalb and say who plays which sport.

examples.de: Ich trainiere, weil ich fit werden will.
examples.en: I train because I want to get fit.
examples.why: You know this already: weil sends the verb to the end.

examples.de: Zuerst laufe ich, dann schwimme ich.
examples.en: First I run, then I swim.
examples.why: You know this already: after zuerst and dann the verb comes next.

examples.de: Ich will fit werden. Deshalb trainiere ich.
examples.en: I want to get fit. That is why I train.
examples.why: New today: deshalb gives the result, and the verb comes right after it.

cards.more: Picture two sentences on two river banks. On the left bank stands the reason: I want to get fit. On the right bank stands the result: I train. With weil you build the bridge inside one sentence, and the verb falls to the end. With deshalb you keep two separate sentences, and the little word deshalb is the bridge between them. After the bridge the verb walks first, then the person. You already walk that path with zuerst and dann.

cards.title: Sport in the WG: who does what
cards.body: Every person in the WG has a sport (die Sportart, plural die Sportarten). Mira plays volleyball in the sports hall, Leon watches handball, Ben runs. Der Spieler plays, der Trainer coaches the team. In handball you score a goal (das Tor). Die Verletzung is an injury; sich verletzen means to get hurt.
cards.lead: Before the new connector you need the people and places of the chapter. This card gives you nine words for sport, so you can talk about who does what, where.

examples.de: Mira spielt Volleyball in der Sporthalle.
examples.en: Mira plays volleyball in the sports hall.
Leon watches handball on TV.
Ben runs in the park.

deeper.text: Words for people with -er have a female form with -in: der Spieler, die Spielerin; der Trainer, die Trainerin. The male plural stays the same (die Spieler), the female plural adds -nen (die Spielerinnen). For a mixed group you often hear Spielerinnen und Spieler. Die Verletzung ends in -ung, so it is always die. Sich verletzen needs the reflexive pronoun you already know.

example.de: Mira hat sich verletzt.
example.en: Mira has hurt herself.

cards.more: Imagine the noticeboard in the WG with three name tags. Under each name hang a sport and a place. Read one line aloud: Mira spielt Volleyball in der Sporthalle. Now swap one piece, like in a card game: Ben spielt Handball im Park. Der Spieler plays, der Trainer shouts the plan, and das Tor is the net where the ball must go, in handball and in football. Sich verletzen means you hurt yourself; die Verletzung is the injury afterwards.
steps: Say who: Mira
Say the sport: spielt Volleyball
Say the place: in der Sporthalle

cards.title: Deshalb: the result word
cards.body: Deshalb means that is why or so. Say the reason first. Then start the second sentence with deshalb. Deshalb sits in position 1, so the verb comes right after it, and the subject follows the verb. Mira has a game tomorrow. Deshalb trainiert sie heute.
cards.lead: Now the new word itself. You use the position-1 idea from zuerst and dann: one word in front, the verb right behind it, then the subject.

examples.de: Mira hat morgen ein Spiel. Deshalb trainiert sie heute.
examples.en: Mira has a game tomorrow. That is why she trains today.

examples.de: Ben will fit werden. Deshalb läuft er jeden Morgen.
examples.en: Ben wants to get fit. That is why he runs every morning.

examples.de: Leon liebt Handball. Deshalb schaut er das Spiel im Fernsehen.
examples.en: Leon loves handball. That is why he watches the game on TV.

deeper.text: Deshalb is an adverb, so it can also move into the middle of the second sentence. Natives often say: Ich will gewinnen. Ich trainiere deshalb jeden Tag. The sentence then keeps its normal order: subject first, verb second, and deshalb right after the verb. The meaning does not change. Starting with Deshalb puts more weight on the result, so use it at the start when you want to stress it.

example.de: Ich will gewinnen. Ich trainiere deshalb jeden Tag.
example.en: I want to win. So I train every day.

cards.more: Build the second sentence like a little train. The engine is deshalb, the first carriage is the verb, the second carriage is the person, and the luggage comes last. Mira trainiert heute turns into Deshalb trainiert sie heute. Compare it with a question: Trainiert sie heute? There too the verb stands in front of the person. The only difference is that deshalb stands in front of the verb, like the engine at the head of the train.
steps: One sentence with the reason
Deshalb in position 1 of the next sentence
The verb right after deshalb
The subject
The rest of the sentence

cards.title: Full stop or comma: the verb stays second
cards.body: You can write a full stop before deshalb, or a comma. Both are correct. In both cases the verb stands right after deshalb. Do not send it to the end like after weil. Wrong: Deshalb ich bleibe zu Hause. Right: Deshalb bleibe ich zu Hause.
cards.lead: Writers often ask: full stop or comma? Both work. This card shows the two options and the one thing that never changes, the verb right behind deshalb.

examples.de: Ich bin müde. Deshalb gehe ich nach Hause.
examples.en: I am tired. That is why I go home.

examples.de: Ich bin müde, deshalb gehe ich nach Hause.
examples.en: I am tired, that is why I go home.

examples.de: Es ist spät, deshalb geht Ben nach Hause.
examples.en: It is late, that is why Ben goes home.

deeper.text: You can add und in front: Es ist spät, und deshalb geht Ben nach Hause. Und is a position-0 word, so deshalb keeps its place and the verb still comes right after it. This sounds very natural in speech, because und gives you a moment to think. After a comma deshalb is written with a small d. In careful writing, two short sentences with a full stop are often clearer.

example.de: Es ist spät, und deshalb geht Ben nach Hause.
example.en: It is late, and so Ben goes home.

cards.more: Think of deshalb as a door and of the verb as a polite guest who always walks through the door first. The person comes in after the verb. It makes no difference if you put a full stop or a comma in front of the door. Two mistakes are common. First: the person walks in first (deshalb ich bleibe). Second: the verb is pushed to the very end, like after weil (deshalb ich zu Hause bleibe). Both are wrong. Say it slowly: deshalb, verb, person.

rows: Ich bin müde, deshalb ich gehe nach Hause.
Ich bin müde, deshalb gehe ich nach Hause.

cards.title: Deshalb, weil, denn: one meaning, three word orders
cards.body: Weil and denn give the reason. Weil sends the verb to the end. Denn is position 0: the order stays normal. Deshalb gives the result: the verb comes right after it. The three sentences below say the same thing in three different ways.
cards.lead: You now have three connectors for one idea. This card puts them side by side, so you can see how the word order changes with each one.

examples.de: Ich trainiere viel, weil ich gewinnen will.
examples.en: I train a lot because I want to win.

examples.de: Ich trainiere viel, denn ich will gewinnen.
examples.en: I train a lot, because I want to win.

examples.de: Ich will gewinnen. Deshalb trainiere ich viel.
examples.en: I want to win. That is why I train a lot.

deeper.text: Warum asks for a reason, so the answer is a weil-clause, not deshalb: Warum trainierst du so viel? – Weil ich gewinnen will. A weil-clause can stand alone as an answer, and the verb still goes to the end. Deshalb cannot answer Warum? alone, because it gives the result, not the reason. So use weil to answer a question and deshalb to join two statements.

example.de: Warum trainierst du so viel? – Weil ich gewinnen will.
example.en: Why do you train so much? – Because I want to win.

cards.more: Ask yourself which sentence you say first. Reason first? Then the second sentence starts with deshalb, and the verb comes right after it. Result first? Then you add the reason with weil (verb at the end) or denn (normal order). English helps a little: so is deshalb, because is weil or denn. A common trap is Deshalb ich nach Hause gehe: after deshalb the verb must not run to the end. That belongs to weil only.

rows: Ich trainiere viel, weil ich gewinnen will.
Ich trainiere viel, denn ich will gewinnen.
Ich will gewinnen. Deshalb trainiere ich viel.

steps: Weil: the verb goes to the END
Denn: normal order, the verb stays second
Deshalb: the verb comes right after it

cards.title: Deshalb with a second verb
cards.body: Deshalb takes position 1, the verb takes position 2, and the second verb stays at the end. With a modal verb you get the infinitive at the end. With the Perfekt you get the participle at the end. You may also hear deswegen and darum: they mean the same, but you only need to recognise them.
cards.lead: Your sentences are not always short. This card shows what happens to modal verbs and the Perfekt after deshalb: the bracket you know stays closed at the end.

examples.de: Ich habe Fieber. Deshalb kann ich nicht spielen.
examples.en: I have a fever. That is why I cannot play.

examples.de: Es hat geregnet. Deshalb haben wir in der Halle trainiert.
examples.en: It rained. That is why we trained in the hall.

examples.de: Mira ist erkältet. Deshalb will sie heute nicht trainieren.
examples.en: Mira has a cold. That is why she does not want to train today.

deeper.text: Deswegen and darum work exactly like deshalb: position 1, then the verb. Deswegen is just as common in speech, darum sounds a bit more casual. Darum can also mean about it or for that: Darum geht es nicht means that is not the point. You will meet this in real life, but for now you only need darum = that is why.

example.de: Es ist kalt. Darum bleiben wir zu Hause.
example.en: It is cold. That is why we stay at home.

cards.more: Think of a sandwich. The top slice is deshalb plus the first verb. The bottom slice is the second verb at the very end. In the middle goes everything else: the person, nicht, the place. Ich habe Fieber. Deshalb kann ich nicht spielen: kann is the top, spielen is the bottom, and ich nicht sits in the middle. With the Perfekt it is the same: haben on top, trainiert at the bottom. The bracket you know from chapter 1 simply stays closed.
steps: Deshalb in position 1
The first verb (kann, haben, will) right after it
The subject
The middle: nicht, the place
The second verb at the very end

cards.title: Mini dialogue: Ben asks Mira
cards.body: Ben meets Mira after training. He asks why she trains so long. Mira answers with a reason and a result with deshalb. Ben says that he wants to get fit, too, and Mira invites him: Dann komm mit! Read the six lines, then learn the two chunks.
cards.lead: Here you hear deshalb in a real conversation. The question Warum? asks for a reason, and the answer contains reason, deshalb and result.

examples.de: Wir haben am Samstag ein Spiel. Deshalb trainieren wir zwei Stunden.
examples.en: We have a game on Saturday. That is why we train for two hours.
I would like to get fit, too.
examples.why: A chunk to learn: Ich möchte fit werden.

examples.en: Then come along!
examples.why: A chunk to learn: Dann komm mit!

deeper.text: Möchte is the soft form of wollen. Ich will can sound blunt, so natives choose Ich möchte when they ask or wish for something politely. Dann komm mit! is an invitation: komm is the du-command, and mit is the separable prefix that goes to the end (mitkommen). The question Warum trainierst du so lange? uses so lange for such a long time.

example.de: Ich möchte auch Volleyball spielen.
example.en: I would like to play volleyball, too.

cards.more: Read the dialogue like a tiny play with two actors. Ben asks Warum?, Mira gives the reason and the result in two sentences, Ben says what he wants, and Mira invites him. Do not translate word by word. Learn the chunks whole: Dann komm mit! means then come along, and Ich möchte auch fit werden means I would like to get fit, too. Listen for the reason first, then for the word deshalb, then for the result.

lessons.title: Trotzdem spielen wir: trotzdem for surprising results
lessons.goal: Say that something happens although there is a problem with trotzdem and talk about a match: win, defeat, draw.

grammar.point: Trotzdem connects two main sentences and gives a result you do not expect. It stands in position 1, so the verb comes right after it, then the subject: Es regnet. Trotzdem spielen wir. Aber is position 0 (Es regnet, aber wir spielen). Trotzdem can also stand after the verb: Wir spielen trotzdem. Deshalb gives the expected result, trotzdem the surprising one.

mistake.why: Trotzdem takes position 1: the verb comes right after it, then the subject.

terms.meaning: still, anyway: it gives a result you do not expect
words like aber and denn do not count as a position; the sentence goes on normally
a draw, when both teams have the same score

cards.title: Before we start: from „deshalb“ to „trotzdem“
cards.body: Mira's team had a hard game on Saturday. It rained, a player was hurt, and the team still did not give up. Last lesson you gave a result you expect with deshalb. Today you learn the word for a result you do not expect: trotzdem.
steps: You already know: deshalb for an expected result (Es regnet. Deshalb bleiben wir zu Hause), position 1, verb next.
New today: trotzdem for a surprising result (Es regnet. Trotzdem spielen wir) and ten words for a match.
By the end you can: say that something happens in spite of a problem and tell the result of a game.

examples.de: Es regnet. Deshalb bleiben wir zu Hause.
examples.en: It is raining. That is why we stay at home.
examples.why: You know this already: deshalb, verb next.

examples.de: Ich bin müde. Deshalb gehe ich nach Hause.
examples.en: I am tired. That is why I go home.
examples.why: You know this already: the expected result.

examples.en: It is raining. Even so, we play.
examples.why: New today: trotzdem, the result you do not expect.

cards.more: Imagine the weather is bad. The result you expect is: we stay at home, so you say deshalb. But Mira's team plays anyway. That is a surprise, and the word for a surprise is trotzdem. It has exactly the same word order as deshalb: the verb right behind it, then the person. So you do not learn a new rule today, only a new meaning. Think of deshalb as a green light and trotzdem as running through the red light.

cards.title: A match: win, defeat, draw
cards.body: After a game you say the result. Three words matter: der Sieg (3:1), die Niederlage (1:3) and das Unentschieden (2:2). A game has two halves (die Halbzeit, plural die Halbzeiten), and der Gegner is the other team. You say the score as drei zu eins.
cards.lead: Before the new connector you need the words for a match. This card gives you five of them, so you can tell how a game ended.

examples.de: Wir haben drei zu eins gewonnen.
examples.en: We won three to one.
We drew.

examples.de: Nach der Halbzeit haben wir verloren.
examples.en: After half-time we lost.

deeper.text: Der Sieg and die Niederlage are nouns, gewinnen and verlieren are the verbs. To say against whom, use gegen with the accusative: Wir haben gegen den Gegner verloren. A woman is die Gegnerin. Das Unentschieden has the same form in the plural. You say zu between the two numbers, and the higher number often comes first for the winner.

example.de: Wir haben gegen den Gegner verloren.
example.en: We lost against the opponent.

cards.more: Think about the final whistle. Your team has more goals: that is ein Sieg. The other team has more: that is eine Niederlage. Both teams have the same number: ein Unentschieden. Read the score as two numbers with zu in the middle: 3:1 is drei zu eins. Then say what you did: Wir haben gewonnen, verloren or unentschieden gespielt. Try it with your own football or handball score from last week.

rows: Wir haben drei zu eins gewonnen.
Wir haben eins zu drei verloren.

cards.title: Trotzdem: the surprising result
cards.body: Trotzdem means still or anyway. It gives a result you would not expect. Like deshalb, it sits in position 1: the verb comes right after it, then the subject. Es regnet. Trotzdem spielen wir. The first sentence is a problem, the second one is the surprise.
cards.lead: Now the new word itself. Its word order is exactly the order you learned for deshalb, so only the meaning is new.

examples.en: It is raining. Even so, we play.

examples.de: Leon ist müde. Trotzdem schaut er das ganze Spiel.
examples.en: Leon is tired. Even so, he watches the whole game.

examples.de: Mira war erkältet. Trotzdem hat sie trainiert.
examples.en: Mira had a cold. Even so, she trained.

deeper.text: Trotzdem says that the second sentence is the opposite of what you would expect after the first. Cold weather usually means no running, so Es ist kalt. Trotzdem läuft Ben is a surprise. Later you will also meet obwohl, which means although and sends the verb to the end: Ben läuft, obwohl es kalt ist. It tells the same story with a different word order.

example.de: Es ist kalt. Trotzdem läuft Ben im Park.
example.en: It is cold. Even so, Ben runs in the park.

cards.more: Trotzdem is the word of surprise. First you say a problem: It is raining. Then you say what happens against all hope: Even so, we play. Put trotzdem first, then the verb, then the person. It is the same train as deshalb, only the passengers are different. A good test: say But still! in English after the first sentence. If But still! fits, you need trotzdem. Use it whenever the second sentence is a surprise.
steps: A problem or a surprise in the first sentence
Trotzdem in position 1
The verb right after it
The subject
The rest

cards.title: Deshalb or trotzdem? The logic test
cards.body: Both words have the same word order, but opposite meanings. Ask: is the result what you expect? Then use deshalb. Is it a surprise? Then use trotzdem. Mira is ill. Deshalb trainiert sie nicht. But: Mira is ill. Trotzdem trainiert sie.
cards.lead: Both connectors look the same in a sentence. This card gives you a simple test to choose the right one every time.

examples.de: Mira ist krank. Deshalb trainiert sie nicht.
examples.en: Mira is ill. That is why she does not train.

examples.de: Mira ist krank. Trotzdem trainiert sie.
examples.en: Mira is ill. Even so, she trains.

examples.de: Das Wetter ist schön. Deshalb spielen wir im Park.
examples.en: The weather is nice. That is why we play in the park.

deeper.text: The test depends on what the speaker thinks is normal. For most people a cold means rest, but a hard-working athlete may say Trotzdem trainiere ich and be proud of it. The same first sentence can take either word, so you choose by the story you want to tell. If you are unsure, ask: would the listener be surprised? Then trotzdem.

example.de: Ben hat keine Zeit. Trotzdem kommt er zum Training.
example.en: Ben has no time. Even so, he comes to training.

cards.more: Use the test in three steps. First read the first sentence. Second ask: what do I expect next? Third compare. If the second sentence says what you expect, use deshalb. If it says the opposite, use trotzdem. Mira is ill: you expect that she stays at home, so Deshalb fits. If she trains anyway, you did not expect it, so you need Trotzdem. The two words never swap places freely: the story decides.
steps: Read sentence 1
Ask: what do I expect?
Expected result: deshalb
Surprise: trotzdem

cards.title: Aber or trotzdem? Position 0 or position 1
cards.body: Aber and trotzdem both show a contrast, but their word order differs. Aber is position 0: the sentence goes on normally with the subject. Trotzdem is position 1: the verb comes next. Es regnet, aber wir spielen. Es regnet, trotzdem spielen wir.
cards.lead: You already know aber from earlier chapters. Trotzdem means almost the same, so this card shows you the difference in word order.

examples.en: It is raining, but we play.
It is raining, even so we play.

examples.de: Leon ist müde, aber er schaut das Spiel.
examples.en: Leon is tired, but he watches the game.

deeper.text: In speech you often hear both words together: Es ist kalt, aber trotzdem trainieren wir. Aber stays in position 0, so trotzdem is still the first word of its clause and the verb follows it. The double contrast sounds strong, a bit like but still. In careful writing one of the two is usually enough, because trotzdem alone already says it.

example.de: Es ist kalt, aber trotzdem trainieren wir.
example.en: It is cold, but we still train.

cards.more: Look at the second part of the sentence. After aber you start with the person: wir spielen. After trotzdem you start with the verb: spielen wir. If you put the person first after trotzdem (trotzdem wir spielen), it is a mistake, because trotzdem already stands in front of the verb. Imagine a queue: aber waits outside the door (position 0), trotzdem stands inside at the front (position 1), and the verb must be next in line.
steps: Aber stands outside: position 0
The subject follows: Es regnet, aber wir spielen
Trotzdem stands in position 1
The verb follows: Es regnet, trotzdem spielen wir

cards.title: Trotzdem in the middle, and more verbs
cards.body: Trotzdem can also stand after the verb: Wir spielen trotzdem. Then the sentence keeps its normal order. With the Perfekt, trotzdem stands before the participle: Wir haben trotzdem gewonnen. At the start it is still position 1: Trotzdem müssen wir mehr üben.
cards.lead: Trotzdem does not always begin the sentence. Here you see it inside the sentence and with modal verbs and the Perfekt.

examples.en: We play anyway.

examples.de: Mira war erkältet, aber sie hat trotzdem trainiert.
examples.en: Mira had a cold, but she trained anyway.
We won anyway.
Even so, we have to practise more.

examples.de: Mira hatte keine Kraft mehr. Trotzdem hat sie weitergemacht.
examples.en: Mira had no strength left. Even so, she kept going.

deeper.text: Aufgeben and weitermachen are separable verbs, so the prefix goes to the end: Wir geben nicht auf. Wir machen trotzdem weiter. The Perfekt is hat aufgegeben and hat weitergemacht. In the middle trotzdem stands before the prefix, not behind it, so the prefix keeps its place at the very end. Wir machen weiter trotzdem sounds odd to a native.

example.de: Wir machen trotzdem weiter.
example.en: We keep going anyway.

cards.more: Trotzdem can sit in two places, like a guest who either greets you at the door or waits inside. At the start it takes position 1, so the verb follows: Trotzdem müssen wir mehr üben. In the middle it comes after the verb: Wir müssen trotzdem mehr üben. The meaning is the same. In the Perfekt it stands in front of the participle, which waits at the end. Use whichever sounds easier to say.
steps: Start of the sentence: Trotzdem + verb + subject
Middle: subject + verb + trotzdem
Perfekt: haben + trotzdem + participle

cards.title: Mini text: after a hard game
cards.body: Am Samstag hatten wir ein Spiel. Zuerst haben wir gut gespielt. Dann hat sich eine Spielerin verletzt. Wir waren erschöpft. Trotzdem haben wir weitergemacht. Am Ende haben wir drei zu eins verloren. Deshalb waren wir traurig.
cards.lead: Now you read all the connectors together in a short text: story words, trotzdem and deshalb, and the Perfekt.

examples.de: Dann hat sich eine Spielerin verletzt.
examples.en: Then a player got hurt.
Even so, we kept going.
That is why we were sad.

deeper.text: Look at the logic in the story. Trotzdem follows the problem (waren erschöpft): continuing is a surprise. Deshalb follows the result (verloren): being sad is what you expect. Most verbs use the Perfekt in a story, but sein and haben often use waren and hatten. So you can tell one story with all connectors and still keep the verb right after each one.

example.de: Am Ende haben wir verloren.
example.en: In the end we lost.

cards.more: Read the text as a chain of six links. First they played well. Then an injury happened. Then everybody was exhausted. Even so, they kept going. At the end they lost, and that is why they were sad. Each sentence adds one step. Find zuerst, dann, trotzdem, am Ende and deshalb. All of them take position 1, so the verb comes right after them. Read it aloud once and clap at every connector.
steps: Zuerst: the start
Dann: the next step
Trotzdem: a surprise
Am Ende: the end
Deshalb: the result

lessons.title: Hoffentlich gewinnen wir! Hope, disappointment and contrasts
lessons.goal: Express hope and disappointment, react to good and bad news and tell a short story with weil, deshalb, aber and trotzdem.

grammar.point: Hoffentlich takes position 1 like deshalb, so the verb comes next: Hoffentlich gewinnen wir! Ich hoffe, dass … and Schade, dass … send the verb to the end. Weil gives a reason (verb at the end), deshalb an expected result and trotzdem a surprising result (verb next), aber a contrast (position 0).

mistake.why: Hoffentlich takes position 1 like deshalb: the verb comes right after it, then the subject.

terms.meaning: hopefully: the short form of Ich hoffe, dass; verb right after it
what a pity that …; the verb goes to the end
chin up! a friendly thing to say after bad news

cards.title: Before we start: from „trotzdem“ to „Hoffentlich …“
cards.body: Leon watches the final in the restaurant „Zum Löwen“. He hopes, he is disappointed, and Herr Ali comforts him. You already say Ich hoffe, dass … and Ich bin enttäuscht. Today you learn short, natural ways to hope, to be sad about a result and to cheer someone up.
steps: You already know: Ich hoffe, dass wir gewinnen (dass, verb at the end) and Ich bin enttäuscht.
New today: Hoffentlich gewinnen wir! (verb next), Schade, dass wir verloren haben, and kind reactions like Kopf hoch!
By the end you can: express hope and disappointment and tell a short story with weil, deshalb, aber and trotzdem.

examples.en: I hope that we win.
examples.why: You know this already: dass sends the verb to the end.

examples.en: I am disappointed.
examples.why: You know this already: a feeling.

examples.en: Hopefully we win!
examples.why: New today: hoffentlich, verb right after it.

cards.more: Hoffentlich is a shortcut. Ich hoffe, dass wir gewinnen needs two parts: a main part and a dass-part with the verb at the end. Hoffentlich gives you one part only, with the normal order and the verb next: Hoffentlich gewinnen wir! It works like deshalb and trotzdem, which you know now: one word in front, the verb right behind it, then the person. Think of hoffentlich as a wish you can say in one breath.

cards.title: Hope: from „Ich hoffe, dass“ to „Hoffentlich“
cards.body: You can hope in four ways. Ich hoffe, dass … sends the verb to the end. Hoffentlich is shorter and takes position 1: Hoffentlich gewinnen wir! Before a game you say Ich drücke dir die Daumen! (der Daumen, thumb) or Viel Glück! Die Hoffnung is the noun; the big prize is die Meisterschaft.
cards.lead: You know hoffen with dass. This card adds the short form hoffentlich and two friendly things to say before a game.

examples.de: Ich hoffe, dass wir das Finale gewinnen.
examples.en: I hope that we win the final.
Hopefully Mira wins the cup.
I keep my fingers crossed for you!
Hopefully we win the championship!

deeper.text: Hoffentlich replaces the whole beginning Ich hoffe, dass, so the verb comes right after it, like after deshalb. You can also answer a question with it alone: Gewinnt Mira? – Hoffentlich! And the opposite is Hoffentlich nicht! The chunk Ich drücke dir die Daumen is literal: I press the thumbs for you. Dir is the person who gets the good wish.

example.de: Verliert Mira? – Hoffentlich nicht!
example.en: Does Mira lose? – Hopefully not!

cards.more: Two ways to hope, one meaning. With dass the verb jumps to the end: Ich hoffe, dass wir gewinnen. With hoffentlich the verb stays up in position 2: Hoffentlich gewinnen wir. The short way is easier, so use it first. Then learn Ich drücke dir die Daumen as one whole sentence for friends. English players cross their fingers, Germans press their thumbs, that is why der Daumen is in the sentence.

cards.title: Disappointment: Schade, dass … and So ein Pech!
cards.body: When the result is bad, you can say how you feel. Ich bin enttäuscht, weil … gives the reason. Schade, dass … says what a pity it is, with the verb at the end. Short reactions are So ein Pech! and Was für ein Pech! Die Mannschaft (the team) can also disappoint you: Sie hat mich enttäuscht.
cards.lead: Good news is easy. This card gives you the language for the bad news after a game: your feelings and short reactions.

examples.de: Ich bin enttäuscht, weil wir verloren haben.
examples.en: I am disappointed because we lost.

examples.de: Schade, dass wir nicht gewonnen haben.
examples.en: What a pity that we did not win.
The team has disappointed me.

deeper.text: Schade! alone is already a full reaction. Schade, dass is a fixed beginning: after dass the verb goes to the end, as you know. To say who disappointed you, use von: Ich bin von der Mannschaft enttäuscht. Die Enttäuschung is the noun and enttäuschen is the verb: Die Niederlage war eine Enttäuschung. Natives use enttäuscht very often after sport, exams and films.

example.de: Ich bin von der Mannschaft enttäuscht.
example.en: I am disappointed in the team.

cards.more: Tell your feeling and give the reason: Ich bin enttäuscht, weil wir verloren haben. Or say only what you think: Schade, dass wir verloren haben. A short cry also works: So ein Pech! Choose the length you like, like choosing between a long text message and a single emoji. After weil and dass the finite verb (haben) always goes to the very end. That rule never changes, even when you are sad.

rows: Ich bin enttäuscht, weil wir verloren haben.
Schade, dass wir nicht gewonnen haben.
So ein Pech! / Was für ein Pech!

cards.title: Reacting and comforting
cards.body: When a friend has bad news, you cheer them up. Kopf hoch! means chin up. Nächstes Mal klappt es bestimmt means next time it will work out. Das ist doch nicht schlimm says that it is not so bad. And Trotzdem habt ihr gut gespielt gives praise. Klappen means to work out.
cards.lead: Now you move from your own feelings to a friend's. This card gives you four kind sentences for bad news.

examples.en: Chin up!
Next time it will work out for sure.
Even so, you played well.

deeper.text: Klappen means that something works out, and it is used with es: Es klappt. Das hat nicht geklappt means that did not work. Das ist doch nicht schlimm uses doch to sound warm, and schlimm means bad or serious. Kopf hoch stays the same for one person or many: you can say it to du and to ihr. Bestimmt means for sure and makes your comfort stronger.

example.de: Das hat leider nicht geklappt.
example.en: Unfortunately that did not work out.

cards.more: Think about how a good friend talks. First comes a short word that lifts the head: Kopf hoch! Then comes a hope for the future: Nächstes Mal klappt es bestimmt. Then comes a compliment: Trotzdem habt ihr gut gespielt. Trotzdem fits here, because losing and still playing well is a surprise. Do not give long speeches. Two short sentences are enough, and a warm voice does the rest.

rows: Kopf hoch! Nächstes Mal klappt es bestimmt.

cards.title: Four connectors, one story
cards.body: You now know four connectors. Weil gives a reason and sends the verb to the end. Deshalb gives the expected result, verb next. Aber is a contrast, position 0. Trotzdem gives a surprising result, verb next. Choose by meaning, then check the verb.
cards.lead: This card puts all four connectors together. The same two facts about Mira show you how each word changes the sentence.

examples.de: Mira hat gewonnen, weil sie gut trainiert hat.
examples.en: Mira won because she trained well.

examples.de: Mira hat gut trainiert. Deshalb hat sie gewonnen.
examples.en: Mira trained well. That is why she won.

examples.de: Mira war verletzt. Trotzdem hat sie gespielt.
examples.en: Mira was hurt. Even so, she played.

deeper.text: You can also start with the reason clause: Weil sie gut trainiert hat, hat Mira gewonnen. Look at the verbs: the weil-clause ends with hat, and then the main verb hat comes right after the comma. The whole weil-clause counts as position 1, so the main verb must be second. You will hear this order a lot in speech and in reports.

example.de: Weil sie gut trainiert hat, hat Mira gewonnen.
example.en: Because she trained well, Mira won.

cards.more: Try the exercise with two gaps. Mira war verletzt. ___ hat sie gespielt. The right word is Trotzdem, because playing when you are hurt is a surprise. Mira hat gut trainiert. ___ hat sie gewonnen. The right word is Deshalb, because training well leads to winning, just as you expect. Ask three questions: reason, expected result or surprise? Then check the verb: weil sends it to the end, the others keep it next.

rows: Mira hat gewonnen, weil sie gut trainiert hat.
Mira hat gut trainiert. Deshalb hat sie gewonnen.
Mira war verletzt, aber sie hat gespielt.
Mira war verletzt. Trotzdem hat sie gespielt.

cards.title: A short race story: in order, with surprises
cards.body: Am Sonntag ist Ben im Park gelaufen. Zuerst war es leicht. Dann hat er sich verletzt. Trotzdem hat er nicht aufgegeben. Am Ende war er erschöpft, aber stolz. Read the story: all the time words take position 1.
cards.lead: Here you tell a whole story in order. You use the time words you know, add trotzdem for the surprise and keep the Perfekt.

examples.en: Then he got hurt.
Even so, he did not give up.

examples.de: Am Ende war er erschöpft, aber stolz.
examples.en: In the end he was exhausted, but proud.

deeper.text: Plötzlich means suddenly. It also takes position 1, so the verb follows: Plötzlich hat es geregnet. A good story has a beginning (zuerst), a change (dann or plötzlich), a surprise (trotzdem) and an end (am Ende). Use the Perfekt for events and war or hatte for states.

example.de: Plötzlich hat es geregnet.
example.en: Suddenly it rained.

cards.more: A story is a line of events, like beads on a string. Each sentence starts with a signal word: zuerst, dann, plötzlich, trotzdem, am Ende. After the signal comes the verb, then the person. Say the story out loud with your own sport and change the person: Mira, Leon, Anna. Keep the order of the signal words, because they are the string. Notice the aber in the last sentence: erschöpft, aber stolz.
steps: Zuerst: how it started
Dann / Plötzlich: what changed
Trotzdem: what surprised you
Am Ende: how it ended

cards.title: Mini dialogue: Leon and Herr Ali in „Zum Löwen“
cards.body: Leon watches the final in the restaurant „Zum Löwen“. He says Sie to Herr Ali. First there is hope, then the result is bad, then disappointment, and Herr Ali comforts him. Read the six lines.
cards.lead: In this dialogue you hear all the new phrases together: hope, a bad result, disappointment and comfort.

examples.de: Hoffentlich gewinnt unsere Mannschaft das Finale!
examples.en: Hopefully our team wins the final!
What bad luck!

deeper.text: Leon says Herr Ali and uses Sie, and Herr Ali answers with Leon's first name: in Germany the older person may use the first name. Ich hoffe es auch uses es for the whole idea that we win. Das ist doch nicht schlimm shows how doch makes a sentence warmer. The path hope, surprise, disappointment, comfort is a typical pattern.

example.de: Ich hoffe es auch.
example.en: I hope so, too.

cards.more: Read the dialogue three times. First understand it. Then cover the right column and say Herr Ali's lines from memory. Then change the story: your team wins, and Herr Ali says Herzlichen Glückwunsch! Look at the order of the story: hope, bad news, feeling, comfort, a positive last word. This order is how real conversations after a match go, so practise the table as a pattern, not word by word.

lessons.title: Ich gebe ihn meinem Bruder: when the thing is a pronoun
lessons.goal: Give, lend and show sports things, and replace the thing with ihn, sie or es in the right place: before the person noun.

grammar.topic: Two objects: the thing as a pronoun comes before a person noun
grammar.point: Verbs like geben, schenken, leihen and zeigen have a person (dative, Wem?) and a thing (accusative, Was?). Two nouns: the person first. A person pronoun: still first (Ich gebe ihm den Ball). When the thing is a pronoun (ihn, sie, es), it comes before the person noun (Ich gebe ihn meinem Bruder). Short word before long word: a pronoun comes before a noun.
grammar.oneLine: Ich gebe ihn meinem Bruder. Leon schenkt es seinem Vater.

mistake.why: A pronoun comes before a noun. The thing is now the small word ihn, so it jumps in front of the person.

terms.meaning: person (Wem?) / thing (Was?)
a small word that replaces a noun: ihn, sie, es
a pronoun comes before a noun

cards.title: Before we start: from „Ich zeige meiner Lehrerin mein Heft“ to „Ich zeige es meiner Lehrerin“
cards.body: After training, Mira has a bag full of jerseys (die Trikots) and water bottles (die Trinkflaschen). The coach (die Trainerin) asks: Who gets what? In earlier chapters you gave things to people with two nouns. Today the thing becomes a small word like es or ihn, and it jumps to a new place in the sentence.
steps: You already know: Ich schenke dir einen Pullover and Ich zeige meiner Lehrerin mein Heft: the person comes first (A1 chapter 11 and A2 chapter 2).
New today: when the thing is a pronoun (ihn, sie, es), it comes BEFORE the person noun.
By the end you can: say Ich gebe ihn meinem Bruder and Leon schenkt es seinem Vater.

examples.de: Leon schenkt seinem Vater ein Trikot.
examples.en: Leon gives his father a jersey.
examples.why: You know this already: the person comes first, then the thing.

examples.en: Leon gives him a jersey.
examples.why: You know this too: a person pronoun is still first.

examples.en: Leon gives it to his father.
examples.why: New today: the thing is now es, so it jumps in front of the person.

cards.more: Picture a queue at a bus stop. A small, quick person like es or ihn always steps to the front. A bigger group like seinem Vater waits behind. German likes short words early in the sentence. You will see this in six small steps: first the sports bag, then the old rule, then the new jump. Nothing is hard if you go one card at a time.

cards.title: A sports bag: things you give, lend and show
cards.body: A sports bag is full of things you hand over: das Trikot (jersey), der Fanschal, die Trinkflasche, die Sporttasche, die Stoppuhr, die Medaille, die Urkunde. Learn the article with each word: you need it later to choose the pronoun. Geben, leihen, schenken, zeigen, werfen and überreichen (to hand over) take a person and a thing.
cards.lead: Before the new rule you need the words. This card gives you the sports things with their articles, and shows who gives what to whom, so the later cards can use them without stopping.

examples.de: Mira gibt der Trainerin den Schlüssel.
examples.en: Mira gives the coach the key.
examples.why: Who gets it: der Trainerin. What: den Schlüssel.

examples.de: Leon schenkt seinem Vater ein Trikot.
examples.en: Leon gives his father a jersey.
examples.why: The person is first, the thing is second.

examples.en: Anna lends Ben her stopwatch.
examples.why: Ben gets it, so Ben is the person. Her stopwatch is the thing.

deeper.text: Most of these words take -n in the plural: die Trinkflaschen, die Sporttaschen, die Stoppuhren, die Medaillen, die Urkunden. The words Trikot and Fanschal take -s: die Trikots, die Fanschals. In the plural the article is always die, and that matters later when you pick a pronoun for the thing.

example.de: In der Sporttasche liegen zwei Trikots.
example.en: Two jerseys are in the sports bag.

cards.more: Think of the sports bag as a shelf with labels. Each thing has a label: der, die or das. Say the label together with the word every time: das Trikot, die Stoppuhr, der Fanschal. Later you will swap the thing for a small word, and the label tells you which one. Say each word aloud three times with its label. Then close your eyes and name five things from your own bag.

cards.title: Two nouns: the person comes first
cards.body: Many verbs have two objects. The person is the dative object: ask Wem? The thing is the accusative object: ask Was? With two nouns, the person comes first, then the thing. You already know this from A1 chapter 11 and A2 chapter 2: Ich gebe meinem Bruder den Ball.
cards.lead: A quick recap, because the new rule grows out of this one. You see the old order of two nouns and the two questions Wem? and Was?, so you can find the person and the thing in any sentence.

examples.de: Ich gebe meinem Bruder den Ball.
examples.en: I give my brother the ball.
examples.why: Wem? meinem Bruder. Was? den Ball.

examples.en: Ben lends Anna his sports bag.
examples.why: Names have no ending, so ask Wem? to find the person.

examples.de: Herr Ali bringt der Mannschaft die Trinkflaschen.
examples.en: Herr Ali brings the team the water bottles.
examples.why: der Mannschaft: the team gets them.

deeper.text: If the person is a name like Anna or Ben, nothing changes on the word, so you cannot see the case. Ask the question: Wem leiht Ben die Tasche? Anna. The answer to Wem? is always the person. The answer to Was? is the thing. This works with every verb that gives, lends, shows or brings.

example.de: Leon zeigt Mira das Foto.
example.en: Leon shows Mira the photo.

cards.more: Imagine a parcel. A parcel has a receiver and something inside. Wem? points at the receiver, Was? points at the thing inside. In German you write the receiver first and the content second when both are nouns. This is the order you already use, so say it three times with different nouns and you are ready for the next card: Ich gebe dem Trainer den Ball, ich gebe der Mannschaft die Flaschen.

Ask Was? to find the thing (accusative)
Two nouns: say the person first, then the thing

cards.title: A person pronoun: still first
cards.body: The person can be a small word: mir, dir, ihm, ihr, uns, euch, ihnen, Ihnen. A person pronoun stays in front of the thing: Ich gebe ihm den Ball. This is the order from A1 chapter 11. Nothing new yet. Use the table to check which small word fits which person.
cards.lead: Now the person becomes a small word. This card lists the person pronouns and shows that they still come first, so that only one thing changes in the next card: the thing.

examples.en: I give him the ball.
examples.why: ihm = to him.

examples.en: Anna lends him her stopwatch.
examples.why: ihm is short, so it stays before the thing.

examples.en: Mira shows you the medal.
examples.why: dir = to you.

deeper.text: The polite word is Ihnen, with a capital I. You use it for Frau Weber or Herr Ali when you speak to them. Do not mix it up with ihnen (to them): you hear no difference, and you see the difference only by the capital letter. Both come first in the sentence, before the thing.

example.de: Ich bringe Ihnen die Rechnung.
example.en: I bring you the bill.
example.why: Polite: Ihnen with a capital letter.

cards.more: Think of a short name tag for each person. mir is the tag for me, dir for you, ihm for him, ihr for her. You do not need a long phrase. The small tag goes where the person goes: right behind the verb. If you already used these words in A1 (Ich schenke dir ...), you are only repeating a friend. Read the table out loud, row by row, and make one sentence for each.

cards.title: New: the thing becomes a pronoun and jumps ahead
cards.body: When the thing (accusative) is a pronoun, it jumps in front of the person noun. The pronoun matches the gender of the thing: der Ball becomes ihn, die Flasche becomes sie, das Trikot becomes es, and a plural becomes sie. Put the pronoun right after the verb, then the person.
cards.lead: This is the new idea of the lesson. You replace the thing with a small word and move it forward. Follow the four steps and the table, and you can do it with any sports thing from the bag.

examples.en: I give it to my brother. (der Ball)
examples.why: ihn replaces der Ball and jumps in front.

examples.en: Leon gives it to his father. (das Trikot)
examples.why: es replaces das Trikot.

examples.en: Mira gives it to the coach. (der Schlüssel)
examples.why: ihn replaces der Schlüssel.

examples.de: Mira wirft den Ball. Leon fängt ihn.
examples.en: Mira throws the ball. Leon catches it.

deeper.text: Why ihn and not er? The thing is the object of the verb, so you need the accusative form: ihn. Sie and es look the same in both cases. The plural pronoun for things is sie, the same word as she. So you must know the noun to understand which sie is meant: one stopwatch or many things.

example.de: Ben leiht sie Anna.
example.en: Ben lends it to Anna. (die Stoppuhr)
example.why: A name has no article, but the pronoun still goes first.

cards.more: Imagine a relay race. The thing is the baton. When the baton is a big word like den Ball, it waits at the back. When it is a small word like ihn, it runs forward and hands itself to the runner right after the verb. Then the person comes last. Do this with four things from the bag and say each sentence aloud before the next card.
steps: Find the thing: ask Was? (den Ball)
Replace it with ihn, sie or es (by gender; plural: sie)
Put the pronoun right after the verb
Then say the person: meinem Bruder

cards.title: The rule in one line: short before long
cards.body: A pronoun comes before a noun. You now know three cases. Two nouns: the person first. Person pronoun and thing noun: the person first, because the pronoun is first. Thing pronoun and person noun: the thing first, because the pronoun is first. The pronoun wins in every case.
cards.lead: Now you have three cases in your head. This card puts them side by side in one table and gives you one easy line to remember: short word before long word.

examples.de: Leon schenkt seinem Vater ein Trikot.
examples.en: Leon gives his father a jersey.
examples.why: Two nouns: the person first.

examples.en: Leon gives him a jersey.
examples.why: Person pronoun first.

examples.en: Leon gives it to his father.
examples.why: Thing pronoun first.

deeper.text: With two nouns the person-first order is the neutral one, but natives sometimes put the thing first to stress the person: Ich gebe den Ball meinem Bruder, nicht meiner Schwester. With a pronoun this switch is not possible: Ich gebe meinem Bruder ihn is always wrong. So the pronoun rule is stricter than the rule for nouns, and you can rely on it every time.

example.de: Ich gebe den Ball meinem Bruder, nicht meiner Schwester.
example.en: I give the ball to my brother, not to my sister.

cards.more: Think of a shelf with small boxes and big boxes. Small boxes (pronouns) always go on the front of the shelf, big boxes (nouns) go behind them. It does not matter whether the small box is the person or the thing. Look at your sentence and ask: is there a small word? Put it first. If there are two nouns, the person goes first. That is all the rule you need today.

rows: Ich gebe meinem Bruder den Ball.

steps: Is there a pronoun? Put it first
Two nouns? The person comes first
Thing pronoun + person noun: the thing comes first

cards.title: Questions and the Perfekt
cards.body: The order stays the same in questions and in the Perfekt. In a yes/no question the verb comes first, then du, then the pronoun and the person. In the Perfekt the participle goes to the end. Learn these three sentences by heart and change the nouns.
cards.lead: So far you have seen statements in the present. This card shows the same new order in a question and in the Perfekt, the two forms you need most in real conversation.

examples.en: Do you give it to your sister? (der Ball)
examples.why: Question: verb first, then du, then ihn.

examples.de: Ich habe es meinem Vater geschenkt.
examples.en: I gave it to my father. (das Trikot)
examples.why: Perfekt: the participle is at the end.

examples.de: Herr Ali hat sie der Mannschaft gebracht.
examples.en: Herr Ali brought them to the team. (die Trinkflaschen)
examples.why: Perfekt: hat, sie, der Mannschaft, gebracht.

deeper.text: To ask who owns something, use the chunk Wem gehört das Trikot? The answer is Es gehört Anna. When you hand something over, you can just say Hier, bitte! Learn both as pieces: Wem gehört ...? and Hier, bitte! You do not need a theory for them today.

example.de: Wem gehört das Trikot?
example.en: Whose jersey is that?
example.why: Learn Wem gehört ...? as one piece.

cards.more: A question is just the statement with the verb moved to the front. Take Ich gebe ihn meinem Bruder, put gebe in front: Gebe ich ihn meinem Bruder? Or with du: Gibst du ihn deiner Schwester? For the Perfekt, take Ich gebe, change it into Ich habe ... gegeben and move the participle to the end. The small pronoun and the person stay where they were.

rows: Ich habe es meinem Vater geschenkt.
Herr Ali hat sie der Mannschaft gebracht.

steps: Question: the verb comes first, then du
Then the thing pronoun and the person
Perfekt: the participle goes to the end

lessons.title: Ich gebe es dir: two pronouns
lessons.goal: Use two pronouns together, the thing first, with all verbs that have two objects: with modal verbs, in the Perfekt, in the imperative and in dass and ob clauses.

grammar.topic: Two pronouns: the thing (accusative) comes before the person (dative)
grammar.point: When both objects are pronouns, the thing comes first, then the person: Ich gebe es dir. Mira gibt ihn ihr. With two nouns the person is first. With one pronoun the pronoun is first. The pronouns stay right after the subject with modal verbs, in the Perfekt, in the imperative and in clauses with dass, ob and weil.
grammar.oneLine: Ich gebe es dir. Kannst du sie mir erklären?

mistake.why: With two pronouns, the thing (accusative) comes first and the person (dative) second.

terms.meaning: with two pronouns the thing is first
a verb with a prefix that splits off: bringt ... bei
you only need to understand it, not to say it yet

cards.title: Before we start: from „Ich gebe ihn meinem Bruder“ to „Ich gebe es dir“
cards.body: Leon needs a Fanschal for Saturday. Mira says: Klar, ich gebe ihn dir! Two small words, no nouns. In the last lesson only the thing was a pronoun. Today both the thing and the person are small words, and you learn which one comes first.
steps: You already know: Ich gebe ihm den Ball and Ich gebe ihn meinem Bruder (lesson 4): a pronoun comes before a noun.
New today: with two pronouns, the thing comes first, then the person.
By the end you can: say Ich gebe es dir, Mira gibt ihn ihr and Kannst du sie mir erklären?

examples.en: I give him the ball.
examples.why: You know this already: person pronoun, then the thing.

examples.en: I give it to my brother.
examples.why: You know this from lesson 4: the thing pronoun jumps ahead.

examples.en: I give it to you.
examples.why: New today: both are pronouns. The thing comes first.

cards.more: Imagine two runners, both small and quick. Who goes first? The one who carries the baton, the thing. The person pronoun follows right behind. It is one clear rule with no exceptions. English says give it to him, with the little word to; German has no such word, the order alone does the job. You will practise it in six small steps: the plain rule, a table with all four cases, new verbs, and the places where the pronouns stay put.

cards.title: Two pronouns: the thing first
cards.body: When the thing and the person are both pronouns, the thing (accusative) comes first and the person (dative) second. Make it in three steps: replace the thing with ihn, sie or es; replace the person with mir, dir, ihm, ihr, uns, euch, ihnen or Ihnen; say the thing, then the person.
cards.lead: You know that a pronoun comes before a noun. Now two pronouns meet in the same sentence, and you need to know which one goes first. This card gives you a three-step way to build it.

examples.en: I give it to you. (das Trikot)
examples.why: Thing first: es. Then the person: dir.

examples.en: Mira shows it to her. (der Schlüssel)
examples.why: ihn comes before ihr.

examples.en: Herr Ali shows it to them. (das Spiel)
examples.why: es, then ihnen.

deeper.text: Why the thing first? When both words are pronouns, German puts the accusative before the dative. You can remember it with the letters: A before D, like in the alphabet. English does it with a little word: give it to him. German has no to, so only the order shows who gets what. This works only with two pronouns. With nouns the order is different, as in lesson 4.

example.de: Leon gibt sie mir.
example.en: Leon gives it to me. (die Stoppuhr)

cards.more: Think of a postman with two small notes. One says what is in the parcel, the other says who gets it. German reads the parcel first and the receiver second: es, dir. If you forget, say it like a short sentence in your head: Thing, person. Then try it with three things from the sports bag and with three people: me, you, him. Say each one aloud.
steps: Find the thing and replace it with ihn, sie or es
Find the person and replace it with mir, dir, ihm, ihr, uns, euch, ihnen or Ihnen
Say the thing first, then the person

cards.title: The full table: four cases
cards.body: Now you know all four cases. Two nouns: the person first. A person pronoun and a noun: the pronoun first. A thing pronoun and a person noun: the pronoun first. Two pronouns: the thing first, then the person. Use the table to check any sentence you build.
cards.lead: Four cases are many to carry in your head. This card puts them in one table with one sports sentence each, so you can look back whenever you build a sentence with two objects.

examples.de: Mira gibt der Trainerin den Schlüssel.
examples.en: Mira gives the coach the key.
examples.why: Two nouns: the person first.

examples.en: Mira gives it to the coach.
examples.why: The thing pronoun is first.

examples.en: Mira shows it to her.
examples.why: Two pronouns: the thing first.

deeper.text: Compare with English: give it to him uses to, but German has no such word, so the order and the case do the work. Look at the pattern in the table. In three of the four cases a pronoun comes first. Only with two nouns do you say the person first, and only with two pronouns the thing first. Read the table from top to bottom and the sentence gets shorter every time.

example.de: Mira gibt ihr den Schlüssel.
example.en: Mira gives her the key.
example.why: Person pronoun with a thing noun: the pronoun first.

cards.more: A table is like a small map. You do not need to learn every cell by heart. You only need to ask two questions: Are there pronouns? Which one is the thing? If there is no pronoun, say the person first. If there is one pronoun, put it first. If there are two, say the thing first. Cover the right-hand column with your hand and build the sentences yourself.

rows: Mira gibt der Trainerin den Schlüssel.

cards.title: More verbs with two objects
cards.body: Four new verbs take a person and a thing: wünschen (Ich wünsche dir viel Glück!), beibringen (Die Trainerin bringt uns die Technik bei), versprechen (Ich verspreche es dir) and reichen (Kannst du mir das Wasser reichen?). They follow the same rules as geben.
cards.lead: You have the order. Now you add verbs that people really use around sport: wishing luck, teaching a technique, promising something and passing a bottle. They all take the same two objects.

examples.de: Die Trainerin bringt uns die Technik bei.
examples.en: The coach teaches us the technique.
examples.why: beibringen is separable: bringt ... bei.

examples.en: I wish you good luck!
examples.why: wünschen: the person is first.

examples.de: Kannst du mir das Wasser reichen?
examples.en: Can you pass me the water?
examples.why: reichen = to pass.

deeper.text: Be careful with the word ihr. It can be the subject (ihr = you all) or the person (ihr = to her). In Gebt ihr es ihr? the first ihr is the subject and the second is the person: Do you all give it to her? You only need to recognise this sentence. You do not need to say it yet.

example.de: Gebt ihr es ihr?
example.en: Do you all give it to her?
example.why: First ihr = you all, second ihr = to her.

cards.more: Think of a toolbox. You already have one tool for giving (geben). Now you add four more tools. They look different, but they work in the same way: a person gets something. Wünschen is for wishes, beibringen is for teaching, versprechen is for promises, and reichen is for passing something along. Try each one with the little words es and dir, then add besorgen, erklären, schicken and empfehlen from the table.

rows: Die Trainerin bringt uns die Technik bei.
Kannst du mir das Wasser reichen?
Kein Problem, ich besorge sie dir.

cards.title: With a modal verb or the Perfekt
cards.body: The two pronouns stay close to the subject. The second verb goes to the end: the infinitive after a modal verb, the participle in the Perfekt. Learn: Kannst du sie mir erklären? Ich habe sie dir geschickt. Willst du es ihm zurückgeben? The thing comes first, the person second.
cards.lead: So far the verb was the only verb. Now there are two verbs, a helper and a second one. This card shows where the pronouns go: they do not travel to the end with the second verb.

examples.en: Can you explain them to me? (die Regeln)
examples.why: The second verb is at the end.

examples.en: I sent them to you. (die Fotos)
examples.why: Perfekt: the participle is at the end.

examples.en: Do you want to give it back to him? (das Trikot)
examples.why: zurückgeben stays together at the end.

examples.de: Die Trainerin hat ihn uns in der Übungsstunde gezeigt.
examples.en: The coach showed it to us in the practice session. (der Aufschlag)

deeper.text: The pronouns do not move, and they stand before nicht: Ich habe ihn dir nicht gegeben. In every sentence the order is: finite verb, subject, thing, person, nicht if you need it, then the second verb. The middle of the sentence stays the same as in the present. Only the end changes. So you can build long sentences by adding one block at a time.

example.de: Ich habe ihn dir nicht gegeben.
example.en: I did not give it to you.

cards.more: Imagine a sandwich. The first verb is the top slice, the second verb is the bottom slice, and the pronouns are the filling in the middle. The filling does not slip out: it is always between the two slices. Make three sandwiches with different fillings: es mir, sie dir, ihn ihm. Change the top slice from kannst to willst to hast and say each sentence aloud.
steps: The first verb (kannst, habe, willst)
The subject, then the thing, then the person
The second verb at the very end

cards.title: Imperative and polite sentences
cards.body: In an imperative the verb is first, then the thing, then the person: Gib ihn mir bitte! Zeig es uns! The same order works in polite sentences with Ihnen: Ich bringe sie Ihnen gleich. The word bitte can come at the end or after the pronouns.
cards.lead: In the gym and at the restaurant you ask for things and offer things. This card gives you the pronoun order for commands and for polite offers, so that you sound natural when you hand something over.

examples.en: Give it to me, please! (der Ball)
examples.why: Imperative: verb first, then ihn, then mir.

examples.en: Show it to us! (das Trikot)
examples.why: es before uns.

examples.en: I will bring it to you right away. (die Rechnung)
examples.why: Polite: Ihnen with a capital letter.

examples.de: Die Ausrüstung? Ich besorge sie Ihnen morgen.
examples.en: The equipment? I will get it for you tomorrow.

deeper.text: The du-form of the imperative drops -st: gib, zeig. Strong verbs change the vowel: Gib ihn mir! (not Geb). For Frau Weber or Herr Ali you use Sie, and the verb comes first with Sie after it: Geben Sie ihn mir bitte! The pronouns keep the order thing first, person second. Sie is the subject, Ihnen is the person: do not mix them up.

example.de: Geben Sie ihn mir bitte!
example.en: Please give it to me! (formal)

cards.more: When you hand a friend a bottle, you say Hier, bitte! When you hand it over politely, you can add the pronouns: Ich gebe sie Ihnen. In both cases you only use short words. That is why the order matters. A short word in the right place sounds better than a long phrase in the wrong place. Practise: Gib ihn mir, bitte. Gib sie ihm, bitte. Zeig es uns, bitte.
steps: Verb first: Gib
The thing: ihn
The person: mir
Bitte at the end or after the pronouns

cards.title: In dass, ob and weil clauses
cards.body: In a clause with dass, ob or weil, the verb goes to the end, but the two pronouns stay right after the subject: Ich hoffe, dass du ihn mir morgen zurückgibst. Ich weiß nicht, ob er es ihr gesagt hat. The thing is first, then the person.
cards.lead: You already use dass, ob and weil clauses with the verb at the end. This card shows that two pronouns fit into them without any change: they sit after the subject, and only the verb moves.

examples.de: Ich hoffe, dass du ihn mir morgen zurückgibst.
examples.en: I hope you will give it back to me tomorrow. (der Fanschal)
examples.why: The verb is at the end. ihn mir comes after du.

examples.de: Ich weiß nicht, ob er es ihr gesagt hat.
examples.en: I do not know if he told her. (das Ergebnis)
examples.why: ob: the verb part hat is at the end.

examples.de: Ich bin froh, weil Leon sie mir gebracht hat.
examples.en: I am happy because Leon brought them to me. (die Trinkflaschen)
examples.why: weil: the helper verb hat is last.

examples.de: Ich weiß nicht, ob die Ersatzspielerin sie uns bringt.
examples.en: I do not know if the substitute will bring them to us. (die Trinkflaschen)

deeper.text: Compare the clause with a main sentence. In the main sentence the verb stays near the front: Du gibst ihn mir zurück. In the clause everything stays in the same order, but the verb moves to the end: dass du ihn mir zurückgibst. A separable verb joins up again at the end: zurückgibst.

example.de: Weißt du, ob sie es uns schickt?
example.en: Do you know if she will send it to us? (das Foto)
example.why: Indirect question: ob, subject, thing, person, verb.

cards.more: Imagine the clause as a box with a lid. In the box you find the connector (dass, ob, weil), the subject, the thing, the person and, at the very end, the verb. You do not change the order of the little words. You only put the verb at the bottom of the box. Build one box with dass, one with ob and one with weil, and compare them.

lessons.title: Super Spiel, Leute! Fan posts and comments
lessons.goal: Understand and write posts and comments in a fan forum: cheer, give your opinion, ask a question and answer it, using deshalb, trotzdem and two objects.

grammar.topic: Fan posts and comments: deshalb, trotzdem and two objects in a thread
grammar.point: A fan post has a headline, the result, your opinion and your hope. Use Ich finde, dass ... for the opinion, trotzdem and deshalb in position 1 (the verb comes next) and Hoffentlich for a hope. In a thread you ask with Weiß jemand, ...? and Hat jemand ...? and answer with two pronouns: Ja, ich kann sie dir geben. Wishes follow the order person then thing: Ich wünsche euch viel Glück!
grammar.oneLine: Hoffentlich gewinnen wir! Ich wünsche euch viel Glück!

mistake.why: The person pronoun comes before the thing.

terms.meaning: a short text in a forum: headline, result, opinion, hope
a fixed phrase you learn as one piece, like stolz auf euch
a post with its comments and answers

cards.title: Before we start: from „Ich gebe es dir“ to a fan comment
cards.body: After the game, Leon wants to write in the fan forum of the Kanal-Haie. He needs to cheer, say what he thinks and ask a question. You already know how to write a short comment and how to give things with two objects. Today you put it all into one fan post.
steps: You already know: Ich finde, dass ... and Ich hoffe, dass ... (earlier chapters and lesson 3), and the two-object order from lessons 4 and 5.
New today: a fan post and its comments, with deshalb, trotzdem and questions and answers in a thread.
By the end you can: read a fan post, write a short comment and answer a question in a thread.

examples.de: Ich finde, dass die Stimmung toll war.
examples.en: I think the atmosphere was great.
examples.why: You know this already: Ich finde, dass ... with the verb at the end.

examples.de: Ich gebe es dir am Samstag.
examples.en: I give it to you on Saturday.
examples.why: You know this from lesson 5: thing first, then person.

examples.de: Die Mannschaft hat verloren, trotzdem jubeln die Fans.
examples.en: The team lost, still the fans cheer.
examples.why: New today: all of this in a fan post, here with trotzdem.

cards.more: A forum is a noticeboard where everybody can pin a note. The first note is the post, the others are comments and answers. Each note is short, so you can use the little building blocks you already know: one opinion, one reason, one hope. You learn it in six steps, from the words of the stadium to a small thread with Leon, Mira and Herr Ali.

cards.title: Fans and the stadium
cards.body: Fans (der Fan, die Fans) watch games in the stadium (das Stadion). They stand in die Fankurve, the fans' end. The league is die Liga, and die Tabelle shows which team is first. Die Schiedsrichterin leads the game. Fans feuern die Mannschaft an and jubeln; the referee pfeift.
cards.lead: Before you read a fan post, you need the words of a stadium. This card gives you the places, the people and three verbs of what happens there: cheering, cheering on and whistling.

examples.de: Die Fans feuern die Mannschaft an.
examples.en: The fans cheer the team on.
examples.why: anfeuern is separable: feuern ... an.

examples.en: Everybody cheers.
examples.why: jubeln = to cheer with joy.

examples.en: The referee whistles.
examples.why: A woman: die Schiedsrichterin. A man: der Schiedsrichter.

deeper.text: Fan is der Fan for men and women; the plural is die Fans. A referee has two forms: der Schiedsrichter and die Schiedsrichterin. Anfeuern is separable: Die Fans feuern die Mannschaft an, and in the Perfekt Wir haben sie angefeuert. Some plurals are irregular: die Stadien, die Ligen, die Tabellen. Learn each plural with its noun.

example.de: Im Stadion jubeln alle.
example.en: In the stadium everybody cheers.

cards.more: Think of a big party in a big room. The Stadion is the room. The Fankurve is the part where the loudest guests stand. The Schiedsrichterin is the person with the whistle who keeps order. The Tabelle is the big board that shows who is winning. Say the words and see the room in your mind. Then say what fans do: feuern an, jubeln. What does the referee do? She pfeift.

rows: Die Fans feuern die Mannschaft an.

cards.title: A fan post: headline, result, opinion, hope
cards.body: A fan post has four main parts: a headline, the result, your opinion and your hope. Two extra sentences make it richer: a contrast with trotzdem and a reason with deshalb. Leon writes in the forum of die Kanal-Haie. Read the table and find all six sentences.
cards.lead: You know the words and the building blocks. Now you see them in one real post, so you can copy the structure when you write your own.

examples.de: Die Mannschaft war am Anfang schlecht, trotzdem hat sie am Ende gewonnen.
examples.en: The team was bad at the start, still it won in the end.
examples.why: trotzdem: position 1, the verb hat comes next.

examples.de: Die Stimmung war super, deshalb bin ich heute sehr glücklich.
examples.en: The atmosphere was great, that is why I am very happy today.
examples.why: deshalb: position 1, the verb bin comes next.

examples.de: Hoffentlich gewinnen wir auch nächste Woche!
examples.en: I hope we win next week too!
examples.why: Hoffentlich ends the post with a hope.

deeper.text: Notice how short the sentences are. A fan post is not a long text. One headline, one result, one opinion, one contrast, one reason, one hope: six sentences are enough. The headline is a cheer: Super Spiel, Kanal-Haie! The opinion uses dass: Ich finde, dass die Fankurve toll war.

example.de: Ich finde, dass die Fankurve toll war.
example.en: I think the fans' end was great.
example.why: The opinion uses dass: the verb is at the end.

cards.more: Think of a post as a sandwich with four layers. The top layer is the headline, the next layer is the result, then comes your opinion and the last layer is your hope. You can add one more small layer with trotzdem or deshalb. If you can write one sentence for each layer, you have a post. Try: Super Spiel! Heute haben wir 28 zu 25 gewonnen. Ich finde, dass wir toll waren. Hoffentlich gewinnen wir wieder!

rows: Ich finde, dass die Fankurve toll war.
Die Mannschaft war am Anfang schlecht, trotzdem hat sie am Ende gewonnen.
Die Stimmung war super, deshalb bin ich heute sehr glücklich.
Hoffentlich gewinnen wir auch nächste Woche!

cards.title: Comment chunks: agree, disagree, cheer
cards.body: Under a post you write short comments. Learn these pieces as they are: Super Spiel! Ich bin ganz deiner Meinung. Das sehe ich anders. Schade, dass ... Trotzdem bin ich stolz auf euch! Wir schaffen das! You do not need to know why stolz takes auf: learn stolz auf as one chunk.
cards.lead: Now you read the comments below the post. This card gives you short pieces for agreeing, disagreeing, feeling sad and cheering, so you can answer in one line.

examples.en: I totally agree with you.
examples.why: A chunk: learn it as one piece.

examples.en: I see that differently.
examples.why: A chunk to disagree politely.

examples.de: Trotzdem bin ich stolz auf euch!
examples.en: Still, I am proud of you!
examples.why: stolz auf ... = proud of ...: learn it as a chunk.

deeper.text: Chunks have a tone. Ich bin ganz deiner Meinung is a polite agreement, and Das sehe ich anders is a polite disagreement: Germans are often direct, but they stay friendly. You can soften it: Das sehe ich ein bisschen anders. And for a quick agreement natives say Genau! or Finde ich auch. After Schade, dass the verb goes to the end, as in lesson 3.

example.de: Das sehe ich ein bisschen anders.
example.en: I see that a bit differently.

cards.more: When you are in a crowd, you do not give a speech. You shout one short phrase. Chunks are shouts that you can use again and again. Learn them like song lines: put one in each hand. Super Spiel! is for good news. Schade! is for bad news. Das sehe ich anders is for a different opinion. Wir schaffen das! is for the next game. Read the table and pick the one that fits your mood.

rows: Trotzdem bin ich stolz auf euch!
Still, I am proud of you!

cards.title: Ask and answer in a thread
cards.body: In a thread you ask the whole group a question and somebody answers. You know indirect questions: Weiß jemand, wann das nächste Spiel ist? To ask for a thing, use Hat jemand ...? The answer can use two objects: Ja, ich kann sie dir geben. Use a pronoun for the thing and the person.
cards.lead: A forum is full of questions. This card shows three question types and the answers that fit, so you can ask for information, ask for a thing and ask for an explanation.

examples.de: Weiß jemand, wann das nächste Spiel ist?
examples.en: Does anybody know when the next game is?
examples.why: Indirect question: the verb ist is at the end.

examples.de: Hat jemand noch eine Karte für Samstag?
examples.en: Does anybody still have a ticket for Saturday?
examples.why: jemand = somebody.

examples.de: Ja, ich kann sie dir geben.
examples.en: Yes, I can give it to you. (die Karte)
examples.why: Two pronouns: sie first, then dir.

deeper.text: Jemand means somebody and takes a singular verb: Hat jemand, not Haben jemand. The opposite is niemand, nobody: Niemand hat noch eine Karte. Answers in a thread stay short and often use pronouns, because everybody knows what the thing is: Ja, ich gebe sie dir. You do not repeat the noun, and the order stays thing first, person second.

example.de: Niemand hat noch eine Karte.
example.en: Nobody has a ticket left.

cards.more: A thread is like a conversation across a big table. One person asks, another answers. The easiest answer begins with Ja and then answers the question directly. Add a small word for the thing and a small word for the person. Take Hat jemand noch eine Karte? and answer: Ja, ich kann sie dir geben. The question has a noun, the answer has two pronouns. Practise with three different things from the bag.

Hat jemand noch eine Karte für Samstag?

cards.title: Write your own comment in four steps
cards.body: Write a comment in four steps: react (Super! or Schade!), give your opinion (Ich finde, dass ...), add a reason or result (weil or deshalb), and end with a hope or a wish (Hoffentlich ... or Ich wünsche euch viel Glück!). In a forum you say du and ihr, and you stay friendly.
cards.lead: You can now read posts and answer questions. This card shows you how to write your own comment in four steps, with a polite style that fits a fan forum.

examples.en: Too bad that we lost.
examples.why: Step 1: react.

examples.de: Ich finde, dass die Fans toll waren.
examples.en: I think the fans were great.
examples.why: Step 2: your opinion.

examples.en: I wish you good luck!
examples.why: Step 4: a wish. The person comes before the thing.

deeper.text: In most fan forums people use du and ihr, even with strangers. That is normal. But stay polite: no insults, no angry words, and only one idea per sentence. A good comment is short and friendly. You can end with a wish to the whole team: Ihr seid super! Wir schaffen das! The word euch is the pronoun for the team.

example.de: Ihr seid super!
example.en: You are great!
example.why: ihr = you (all): the team or the fans.

cards.more: Think of a little recipe with four ingredients. First a small cheer, then your opinion, then the reason, then a wish. If you leave one ingredient out, the comment still works. If you add too many, it gets too long. Four short sentences are perfect. Try it now: React: Super Spiel! Opinion: Ich finde, dass wir gut waren. Reason: Die Stimmung war toll, deshalb war ich glücklich. Wish: Ich wünsche euch viel Glück!

Die Stimmung war toll, deshalb war ich glücklich.

steps: React: Super! or Schade!
Opinion: Ich finde, dass ...
Reason or result: weil or deshalb
Hope or wish: Hoffentlich ... or Ich wünsche euch ...

cards.title: A mini thread: Leon, Mira and Herr Ali
cards.body: Here is a small thread. Leon writes a post. Mira answers: she has a ticket. Herr Ali offers to show the next game in „Zum Löwen“. Read the three lines: you see a hope, two pronouns and a polite offer. Everything you have learned in this chapter is in these short lines.
cards.lead: At the end of the lesson you see how the pieces fit together in a real thread. Leon posts, Mira answers with two pronouns, and Herr Ali offers to show the game.

examples.de: Hoffentlich gewinnen wir auch am Samstag!
examples.en: I hope we win on Saturday too!
examples.why: Leon's post: a hope.

examples.en: I still have a ticket.
examples.why: Mira answers Leon.

examples.de: Ich zeige es euch auf dem großen Bildschirm.
examples.en: I will show it to you on the big screen.
examples.why: Herr Ali: es before euch.

deeper.text: Notice how every line is short and ends with something useful: a hope, an offer, a ticket. The best forum posts help somebody. Herr Ali does not write a long text. He says what he does and when. You can do this too: Ich zeige es euch. Ich gebe sie dir. Ich bringe sie Ihnen. The small words do all the work.

example.de: Ich gebe sie dir am Samstag.
example.en: I give it to you on Saturday. (die Karte)

cards.more: Imagine a noticeboard in the stadium with three notes. The first note is a hope, the second is an offer, the third is a promise. Each note is short and friendly. When you read a thread, look for these three types: hope, offer and promise. When you write one, you do the same. Choose a game of your own, and write three notes in your head. Then say them aloud.
