lessons.title: Rennen, Lauf, Rekord: competitions and the sounds r and l
lessons.goal: Talk about competitions and races, and hear and say the German r and l clearly

grammar.topic: competition words; the German sounds l and r; the separable verb teilnehmen
grammar.point: The German l is always clear (tongue tip behind the top teeth). The r at the start of a syllable is made in the throat; after a vowel at the end it is a short uh: Läufer, Trainer, Tor. One sound changes the word: Rand – Land. Separable teilnehmen: Anna nimmt am Stadtlauf teil.

mistake.why: teilnehmen is separable: nimmt stays in position 2 and teil goes to the very end.

terms.meaning: the German l: tongue tip behind the top teeth, never dark
the r at the start of a syllable, made at the back of the mouth
two words that differ in one sound only, like Rand – Land

cards.title: Before we start: from a fan comment to the start line
cards.body: In lesson 6 you wrote fan comments. Now you go to the start line: Anna runs her first Stadtlauf in Hamburg. Today you learn the words of a race and two sounds that make German sound German: l and r. Rand (edge) and Land (country) differ only in that sound.
steps: You already know: Mira spielt Volleyball. and Trotzdem haben wir gewonnen. from lessons 1 to 6.
New today: Anna nimmt am Stadtlauf teil. and the competition words, the clear German l and the throat r.
By the end you can: talk about a race and say Rand – Land, Reise – leise and Läufer clearly.

examples.en: Mira plays volleyball.
examples.why: You know this already.

examples.en: Still, we won.
examples.why: You know this already: trotzdem, then the verb.

examples.en: Anna takes part in the city run.
examples.why: New today: the little word teil goes to the end.

cards.more: Think of a sports day. First you sign up and get a number. Then you run. Then you cross the line and everybody cheers. Today you learn the German words for all of this. You also learn two tiny sounds. The l is bright and the r sits in your throat. If you say them wrong, a word can change: Rand is an edge, Land is a country. One card at a time.

cards.title: Competition words: before, during and after the race
cards.body: A competition is der Wettkampf or der Wettbewerb; a race is das Rennen. Before the start you get die Startnummer and you take part: am Stadtlauf teilnehmen. During the race you run die Runden and überholen other Läufer. After die Ziellinie you may have der Rekord, a record.
cards.lead: Anna runs her first Stadtlauf in this chapter. After the fan words of lesson 6 you now get the words of the race itself, in the order of the day: before, during and after.

examples.en: Anna has a race number.
Anna takes part in the competition.

examples.de: In der letzten Runde überholt Anna eine Läuferin.
examples.en: In the last lap Anna overtakes a runner.
On your marks, get set, go!
examples.why: Call it at the start of every race.

deeper.text: Teilnehmen is separable and a bit irregular: nehmen becomes nimmt. Anna nimmt am Stadtlauf teil: nimmt is in position 2 and teil goes to the very end. In the Perfekt it is Anna hat am Stadtlauf teilgenommen. Wettkampf and Wettbewerb both mean competition, but Wettkampf is mostly sport, and Wettbewerb is wider, for example a drawing contest.

example.de: Anna hat am Stadtlauf teilgenommen.
example.en: Anna took part in the city run.

cards.more: Imagine the race day as a film with three scenes. Scene one: you pick up your number and sign up, so you take part. Scene two: the starting shot, the laps, and you overtake other runners. Scene three: the finish line and the record you hope for. Each scene has its own words, and you learn them in the order of the film. Say one sentence per scene about Anna, then put yourself in the main role.

rows: Anna kommt an der Ziellinie an.

steps: Say who: Anna
Say nimmt in position 2
Say what: am Stadtlauf
Put teil at the very end

cards.title: The German l is always clear
cards.body: The German l is always bright. Put the tip of your tongue behind your upper front teeth, as in la. It never goes dark like the English l in ball or full. So Lauf, Läufer, Halle, Ball and schnell all keep the same clear l, at the start, in the middle and at the end.
cards.lead: You know the race words. Now you say them. Start with the sound that is in Lauf, Läufer and Volleyball: the German l, which is the same bright sound in every place.

examples.de: Mira spielt Volleyball in der Halle.
examples.en: Mira plays volleyball in the hall.
examples.why: Halle and Ball: bright l, tongue tip up.

examples.en: The runner is fast.
examples.why: schnell: the l at the end stays bright.

examples.en: Run, Anna, run!
examples.why: Lauf: l at the start, tongue behind the teeth.

deeper.text: A dark English l pulls the back of the tongue down and sounds a bit like w. In German the tongue stays flat and only its tip touches the teeth, even in the middle and at the end: schnell, Ball, viel. Say the word, hold the l and check: tip up, no w sound.

example.de: Die Halle ist voll.
example.en: The hall is full.

cards.more: Say la, la, la and feel where your tongue sits: the tip touches the little ridge just behind your top teeth. That is the German l. Now say Ball and keep the tip up until the very end. English drops the tongue, so a tiny w or oo sneaks in before the l. German does not let it in. Use a mirror: say Halle and look. If the tip of the tongue lifts at the end, it is German.

cards.title: The German r at the start of a syllable
cards.body: At the start of a word or syllable the German r is made in the throat, like a soft gargle: Rennen, Rekord, Runde, Reise. In the south many people roll it with the tip of the tongue instead. Both are correct. Do not use the English r with rounded lips.
cards.lead: You know the clear l. Now its partner: the r. Races, records and laps all start with it, so you will say it often today.

examples.en: The race starts on Sunday.
examples.why: Rennen: r in the throat.

examples.en: That is a new record!
examples.why: Rekord: r at the start, in the throat.

examples.de: Die Reise nach Hamburg ist lang.
examples.en: The trip to Hamburg is long.
examples.why: Reise: the r is not rounded.

deeper.text: Say a long k in the back of your mouth, ka, then let it turn soft: kh, rh. That feeling is the German throat r. Do not roll the tongue unless you like it. If your r sounds like the English r (lips round), open your lips and move the sound back.

example.de: Die Runde ist lang.
example.en: The lap is long.

cards.more: Imagine a tiny sip of water at the back of your throat. You are about to gargle, but very softly. That quiet vibration is the German r. It should feel like a purr, not a growl. Start with the kh sound of ach, then let your voice join in: rh. A rolled r with the tip of the tongue works too, as many people in the south say it. Only avoid the English r with round lips, because it sounds foreign everywhere.

rows: a soft gargle at the back of the mouth
tip of the tongue taps, common in the south
lips round: not used in German

steps: Start with the kh sound of ach

cards.title: The r after a vowel sounds like uh
cards.body: After a vowel at the end of a syllable the r nearly disappears. It sounds like a short, open uh: der, vier, Tor. The ending -er is uh too: Läufer, Trainer, Spieler. Before a vowel the r stays strong: Läufer, but Läuferin with a throat r.
cards.lead: You can say r at the start of a word. In Läufer, Trainer and Tor the r comes after a vowel at the end. Here it is something else: it turns into a soft uh.

examples.de: Der Läufer ist schneller als der Trainer.
examples.en: The runner is faster than the coach.
examples.why: Läufer, schneller, der, Trainer: all end in uh.

examples.en: The runner has four laps.
examples.why: vier: uh at the end. Läuferin: strong r before i.

examples.en: The coach sees the goal.
examples.why: Tor: the r after the vowel is only uh.

deeper.text: Compare Läufer and Läuferin. In Läufer the r is at the end, so you say uh. In Läuferin an i follows, so the r is a real throat r again. The same happens in Spieler and Spielerin and in Trainer and Trainerin. A vowel after the r brings the strong r back.

example.de: Die Spielerin und der Spieler gewinnen.
example.en: The female player and the male player win.

cards.more: The r is shy at the end of a syllable. It does not growl, it only whispers a short uh. Say Tor like toe plus a quick uh, and der like day plus a quick uh. The ending -er works the same way, so Läufer, Trainer and Spieler all end in a soft uh. When a vowel follows, as in Läuferin, the r wakes up and is strong again, because it starts a new syllable.
steps: r before a vowel: strong throat r (Läuferin)
r after a vowel at the end of a syllable: short uh (Läufer)

cards.title: r or l? Six word pairs
cards.body: Only one sound is different, but the meaning changes. That is why r and l matter. Listen for the throat r and the clear l in each pair: Rand – Land, Reise – leise, Rippe – Lippe, Glas – Gras, Rose – Lose, Ratte – Latte.
cards.lead: You now know two sounds that sound alike to many learners. Six word pairs show why the difference matters: a different sound gives a different word.

examples.de: Das Glas steht auf dem Tisch.

examples.de: Die Halle liegt am Rand von Hamburg.

deeper.text: Practise a pair slowly. For the r word the sound is in your throat. For the l word the tip of your tongue touches your teeth. Then say the pair three times fast. Be careful with two pairs: die Lose are lottery tickets, and die Latte is a slat, a thin wooden bar. A wrong sound can give you a very different word, so slow and clear is better than fast.

example.de: Auf der Reise sind wir leise.
example.en: On the trip we are quiet.

cards.more: Two words, one tiny difference. Think of two buttons on a machine. One button is the throat r, the other is the clear l with the tongue tip up. Press the wrong one and the machine serves a different word: you wanted the edge, but you ordered the country. Say each pair slowly, twice, and feel which button you press. Then record yourself on your phone and listen: can you hear the difference between Glas and Gras?

cards.title: Anna's plan for the race
cards.body: Anna writes her plan for the race. Read it aloud and listen for r and l: Der Lauf ist lang, deshalb trainiere ich viel. Ich bin nervös. Trotzdem nehme ich am Stadtlauf teil. Ben leiht mir seine Stoppuhr. Er gibt sie mir am Freitag.
cards.lead: Words, sounds and pairs are ready. Now you see them together in Anna's plan, with deshalb, trotzdem and two objects from the first lessons of this chapter.

deeper.text: Notice the two objects. Ben leiht mir seine Stoppuhr: person first, because Stoppuhr is a noun. Er gibt sie mir: both are pronouns, so the thing comes first. Notice, too, how Anna uses deshalb and trotzdem in one plan: deshalb for a result she expects (a long run, so she trains), trotzdem for a surprise (she is nervous, but she starts). Her plan is the whole chapter in four sentences.

example.de: Der Lauf ist lang, deshalb trainiere ich viel.
example.en: The run is long, that is why I train a lot.

cards.more: Anna is nervous, but she runs anyway: that is trotzdem. She trains a lot because the run is long: that is deshalb. She also borrows Ben's stopwatch, and Ben gives it to her on Friday. Read the plan aloud like a short speech before the start. Listen for the bright l in Lauf and lang, the throat r in trainiere and the soft uh at the end of Stoppuhr. Then say it again, faster, as if the starting shot is about to go.

lessons.title: Nach dem Wettbewerb: reading a difficult text
lessons.goal: Read a sports article above your level and understand the main points without translating every word

grammar.topic: six steps for a difficult text; compound words; deshalb and trotzdem in a real text (Perfekt)
grammar.point: Read in six steps: headline, W-questions, key words, international words, split compounds, guess from context. In a long compound word the last part is the main word and gives the article: die Siegerin → die Stadtlaufsiegerin. Look up at most three words.

mistake.why: The main word comes last and gives the article: die Siegerin, so die Stadtlaufsiegerin.

terms.meaning: to skim a text quickly for the main points
a key word you know that carries the message
a long word built from short words; the last part gives the article

cards.title: Before we start: from Anna's race plan to the newspaper after the race
cards.body: After the race the newspaper tells the story. Sports articles are full of words you do not know, but you can still understand the main points. You already know die Überschrift, der Absatz and berichten from A2 chapter 4. Today you meet die Schlagzeile, das Schlüsselwort and überfliegen, and you read an article above your level.
steps: You already know: Überschrift, Absatz and berichten from the blog lessons.
New today: Schlagzeile, Schlüsselwort and überfliegen, a six-step plan for a difficult text.
By the end you can: read a short sports article and say what happened without looking up every word.

examples.de: Die Überschrift steht über dem Text.
examples.en: The title is above the text.
examples.why: You know this already.

examples.de: Die Zeitung berichtet über den Stadtlauf.
examples.en: The newspaper reports on the city run.
examples.why: You know berichten.

examples.en: The headline is big.
examples.why: New today: the big headline of a newspaper.

cards.more: A difficult text is like a foggy road. You cannot see everything, but you can see enough to drive. You do not need every word. You need the road signs: the headline, the names, the numbers and the words you already know. Today you get six steps that always work, in a newspaper, on a poster or in an email. Each step is small. Do them in order and the fog lifts bit by bit.

cards.title: Steps 1 and 2: the headline and the W-questions
cards.body: Step 1: look at the Schlagzeile and the photo and guess the topic. Step 2: überfliegen. Read the text fast, once, only to find the answers to Wer? Was? Wann? Wo? Do not stop at words you do not know. The headline already answers some of the questions.
cards.lead: You know what a difficult text is. Now the first two of six steps: guess from the headline, then skim the text once, quickly, and collect the W-answers.

examples.de: Stadtlauf in Hamburg: Sonne, Rekord und viele Fans
examples.en: City run in Hamburg: sun, record and many fans
examples.why: This is the Schlagzeile of our article.

examples.en: Who won? The winner.
examples.why: Wer? asks for a person.

examples.de: Wann war der Lauf? Am Sonntag.
examples.en: When was the run? On Sunday.
examples.why: Wann? asks for the time.

deeper.text: Skimming is not slow reading. Your eyes run over the text and look for names, numbers, places and times. German helps here, because every noun starts with a capital letter, so people and things jump out of the line. The first paragraph often answers most W-questions. Do not translate: ask Wer? Was? Wann? Wo? in your head.

example.de: Wo ist der Lauf? In Hamburg.
example.en: Where is the run? In Hamburg.

cards.more: Imagine you jog past a shop window. You cannot read every price, but you see the big sign, the photo and the colours, and that is enough to know it is a bakery. Überfliegen works the same way. Read once, fast, and ask only four questions: who, what, when, where. The headline and the photo already answer some of them. Do not stop at a word you do not know: your eyes keep running.

rows: not in the headline: look in the text (am Sonntag)

steps: Step 1: look at the Schlagzeile and the photo, guess the topic
Step 2: überfliegen once, fast, and find Wer? Was? Wann? Wo?

cards.title: Steps 3 and 4: key words and international words
cards.body: Step 3: mark the Schlüsselwörter, the words you know that carry the message: Stadtlauf, Hamburg, Rekord, Fans. Step 4: international words look almost the same in English: Marathon, Team, Training, Finale, Fan. They are safe anchors, and you also get the article.
cards.lead: After the headline and the first quick read, you mark what you understand. Key words and international words give you the skeleton of the text.

examples.de: Das Team trainiert für das Finale.
examples.en: The team trains for the final.
The marathon is a competition.

examples.de: Die Fans sehen das Finale im Stadion.
examples.en: The fans watch the final in the stadium.

deeper.text: Be careful with false friends, words that look the same but mean something different. Most sports words are safe, but Handy is a mobile phone, not a hand, and das Gymnasium is a kind of school, not a gym. If the meaning does not fit the sentence, do not trust the look-alike. Check it against the context, which is step 6.

example.de: Das Training beginnt um acht Uhr.
example.en: The training starts at eight o'clock.

cards.more: A key word is a word you already know. Imagine putting a small dot under each one with a pencil. After a minute the dots form a path through the text, and you can follow it like stepping stones across a stream. International words are free stones: Marathon, Team and Finale look like English, and the table gives you the article, too. Mark five dots before you start to worry about the rest.
steps: Step 3: mark the words you already know
Step 4: spot the international words
Use both as anchors and ignore the rest

cards.title: Step 5: split long compound words
cards.body: German builds long words from short ones. Split them: Stadtlaufsiegerin = Stadt + Lauf + Siegerin. The last part is the main word and gives the article: die Siegerin, so die Stadtlaufsiegerin. The first parts only tell you more: a winner of the city run.
cards.lead: The headline and the key words are done. Now the long words that frighten learners. A long word is only short words in a row, and its last part gives the meaning and the article.

examples.en: The winner of the city run laughs.
The spectator record is new.

examples.de: Die Siegerehrung ist um vier Uhr.
examples.en: The award ceremony is at four o'clock.

deeper.text: Work from the back. Zuschauerrekord: the last part is Rekord, so the word is a record. Which kind? A record of the Zuschauer, the spectators. Sometimes a small joining letter sits between the parts, for example Arbeit-s-platz: ignore it when you split the word. The plural also comes from the last part: die Siegerin gives die Stadtlaufsiegerinnen.

example.de: Die Wettkampfstrecke ist lang.
example.en: The competition route is long.

cards.more: Think of building blocks. Each block is a small word you know: Stadt, Lauf, Siegerin. German sticks them together without spaces. To read a long word, take the blocks apart again, starting from the right. The block on the right is the boss: it tells you what the thing is and which article to use. The blocks on the left only describe it. A Stadtlaufsiegerin is a Siegerin, but a special one: the winner of the Stadtlauf.
steps: Split the long word into short words
Find the last part
Take the article from the last part

cards.title: Step 6: guess from the context
cards.body: Step 6: when a word is new, read the sentence around it, the Zusammenhang. Ask what fits. Then guess (erraten). Look up at most three words in the dictionary, only those without which you cannot understand the text. All others you can leave.
cards.lead: Steps 1 to 5 clear most of the text. A few words remain. For them you use your last tool: the clues in the sentences around them.

examples.de: Anna lacht und ruft Super! Sie ist begeistert.
examples.en: Anna laughs and shouts Super! She is thrilled.
examples.why: Clues: lacht, Super! → begeistert is positive.

examples.de: Es ist sehr heiß. Die Läufer schwitzen.
examples.en: It is very hot. The runners sweat.
examples.why: Clues: heiß, Läufer → schwitzen = to sweat.

examples.en: The spectators clap and cheer.
examples.why: Clue: jubeln, so klatschen is a happy action.

deeper.text: Context works in two ways. The words before and after give you a topic, and the grammar gives you the kind of word: after ein and an adjective a noun follows, after ich a verb. Together this narrows the guess. If you still do not know, your guess may be enough.

example.de: Anna ist müde, aber begeistert.
example.en: Anna is tired but thrilled.

cards.more: It is a detective game. The unknown word is the suspect, and the clues are the other words in the sentence. It is very hot, and the runners are in the sun: the new word probably has to do with sweating. You do not have to be sure. A good guess is enough to read on, and the next sentences often confirm it. Write your guess in the margin with a question mark, then see whether the text agrees.

Ask what fits the clues

cards.title: The article: Nach dem Wettbewerb
cards.body: Here is the newspaper text. Read it once, fast, with the six steps: headline, W-questions, key words, international words, compounds, context. The text uses the Perfekt for the past and, in some places, deshalb and trotzdem. Do not look up more than three words.
cards.lead: Now you use all six steps on a real sports article. It is written for readers above your level, so expect some new words.

examples.de: Deshalb war die Stimmung an der Strecke fantastisch.
examples.en: That is why the atmosphere on the route was fantastic.
examples.why: deshalb at position 1, verb next.

examples.en: Still, she ran.
examples.why: trotzdem at position 1, verb next.

examples.de: Am Ende ist sie über die Ziellinie gekommen.
examples.en: In the end she crossed the finish line.
examples.why: Perfekt with sein: ist … gekommen.

deeper.text: The article tells the past with the Perfekt, as people do in speech: hat geschienen, hat geschafft, ist gelaufen. Many newspapers prefer the Präteritum (schien, schaffte), which you will learn later; only war is the same everywhere. Look at deshalb and trotzdem in the text: the verb comes right after them, exactly as in the first lessons of this chapter.

example.de: Ihre Leistung war toll.
example.en: Her performance was great.

cards.more: Read the text like a short film. First the big picture: a run in the sun with many fans. Then the winner and her record. Then Anna: she was nervous, but she ran, and in the end she is thrilled. Use the six steps one after the other and notice how much you already understand. Every key word you know is a stone in the stream. Look up three words at most, and only if a sentence stays unclear.

rows: Stadtlauf in Hamburg: Sonne, Rekord und viele Fans

Hamburg. Am Sonntag war in Hamburg der große Stadtlauf. Das Wetter war perfekt: Die Sonne hat geschienen, und viele Fans haben die Läufer angefeuert. Deshalb war die Stimmung an der Strecke fantastisch.

Die Stadtlaufsiegerin hat die zehn Kilometer sehr schnell geschafft. Ihre Zeit ist ein neuer Rekord. Sie hat Blumen und einen Pokal bekommen. Bei der Siegerehrung hat sie gesagt: „Ich bin so glücklich!“

Auch Anna hat zum ersten Mal am Stadtlauf teilgenommen. Sie war sehr nervös und hat nicht gut geschlafen. Trotzdem ist sie gelaufen. Am Ende ist sie über die Ziellinie gekommen. Ein Reporter hat sie gefragt: „Wie war der Lauf?“ Anna hat geantwortet: „Ich bin müde, aber begeistert!“ Ihre Leistung war toll.

Skim once for Wer? Was? Wann? Wo?

cards.title: Check your understanding
cards.body: After reading, check yourself. Decide for each sentence: richtig or falsch? Then ask the last question: Was ist die wichtigste Information? One short sentence in your own words is the best summary: Anna hat zum ersten Mal am Stadtlauf teilgenommen, und sie ist begeistert.
cards.lead: You have read the article. The last step is to test yourself: which sentences are true, and what is the most important information in the text?

examples.why: This is the last sentence she says to the Reporter.

deeper.text: Two chunks help with a first look at a text: Auf den ersten Blick … means at first glance, and Im Großen und Ganzen … means on the whole. You only need to recognise them. When you read Im Großen und Ganzen, a summary follows. It is a good sign that the author is about to say the most important thing.

example.de: Im Großen und Ganzen war der Lauf toll.
example.en: On the whole, the run was great.

cards.more: After a hard text you have two small jobs. First check single facts: is the sentence richtig or falsch, and where in the text can you prove it? Second, say the whole story in one sentence, like a headline for a friend. If you can do both, you have understood the text, even if some words stayed new. A real exam asks for exactly these two things, so practise them every time you read something.

grammar.point: A report has Überschrift, Einleitung, Hauptteil and Schluss. Tell events in order with zuerst, dann, danach, plötzlich, am Ende: the time word is in position 1 and the verb comes right after it. Use the Perfekt: fahren, laufen and ankommen take sein, most other verbs take haben. Use deshalb for an expected result and trotzdem for a surprising one.

cards.title: Before we start: from the newspaper to your own report
cards.body: The newspaper told Anna's story from the outside. Now you tell your own: a travel report. You know Zuerst sind wir … gefahren from the blog lessons. Today you add the words of a sports trip, the structure of a report and an invented place for sport: die Halle am Kanal.

By the end you can: write a short report with a beginning, three events in order, a contrast and an end.

cards.more: A good report is like a short film in four scenes: the title, the start, the main part and the end. Each scene has its own words. You tell what happened in the order it happened, like numbers on a map: first, second, third. Then you add a surprise (trotzdem), a reason (deshalb) and your feeling, and your text comes alive. Your reader was not there, so you take them by the hand.

cards.title: Travel words for a sports trip
cards.body: A trip to a competition has four parts. Die Anreise is the journey there. Then you sleep in die Unterkunft, for example die Jugendherberge (youth hostel). You feel die Atmosphäre at the race. Then comes die Rückreise, the journey back. Each word has its place in a report.
cards.lead: You know the race words. A trip to a race also needs words for the journey. They follow the order of your trip: there, stay, race, back.

examples.en: The journey there was long.
The accommodation is a youth hostel.

examples.de: Die Atmosphäre in Hamburg war toll.
examples.en: The atmosphere in Hamburg was great.
The journey back was quiet.

deeper.text: Anreise and Rückreise are built from Reise: an means on the way there, zurück means back. You know Hinfahrt and Rückfahrt: die Fahrt is the single ride in a vehicle, die Reise is the whole trip with everything around it. Anreise is a bit more formal and you often read it on event websites and in hotel mails: Anreise mit dem Zug.

example.de: Die Anreise und die Rückreise waren lang.
example.en: The journey there and the journey back were long.

cards.more: Draw a line on paper. On the left is your home, on the right the city of the race. The way to the right is die Anreise. In the city you sleep in die Unterkunft, you feel die Atmosphäre and you run. Then you go back along the line to the left: that is die Rückreise. Four stops, four words. Tell the line aloud and point at each stop.
steps: Die Anreise: the way there
Die Unterkunft: where you sleep
Die Atmosphäre: what you feel at the race
Die Rückreise: the way back

cards.title: The structure of a travel report
cards.body: A report has four parts: Überschrift, Einleitung (wohin, wann, mit wem), Hauptteil and Schluss. In the Hauptteil you tell in order: zuerst, dann, danach, plötzlich, am Ende. The time word is in position 1, so the verb comes right after it. Use the Perfekt: fahren, laufen, ankommen go with sein, most other verbs with haben.
cards.lead: You have the travel words. Now the plan of the whole text: what goes where, and which time words and verbs tell the events in order.

examples.de: Wir sind mit dem Zug nach Hamburg gefahren.
examples.en: We travelled to Hamburg by train.
After that we slept for a long time.
examples.why: Time word in position 1: haben, then wir.

examples.en: Suddenly it rained.
examples.why: Plötzlich = suddenly. Position 1, verb next.

deeper.text: Sein or haben? Use sein when someone moves from one place to another or changes: ist gefahren, ist gelaufen, ist angekommen. Three more verbs also take sein: sein, bleiben and werden (ist geblieben). Most other verbs take haben: hat geschlafen, hat geregnet, hat gewonnen. You know this from the Perfekt. Check it again when you write.

example.de: Am Ende sind wir glücklich angekommen.
example.en: In the end we arrived happily.

cards.more: Imagine you tell a friend about your trip. First you say where you went and with whom. Then you tell what happened first, second and third. At the end you say how you feel. A report is exactly that, but written down. The four parts are four breaths of the story: title, start, middle, end. Check every event sentence: the time word comes first, and the verb follows right behind it.
steps: Überschrift: a short title, for example Unser Wochenende in Hamburg
Einleitung: wohin, wann, mit wem
Hauptteil: zuerst, dann, danach, plötzlich, am Ende
Schluss: your feeling and a hope

cards.title: Contrasts and results in a report
cards.body: A report becomes lively with a contrast and a result. trotzdem and deshalb connect two main sentences, and the verb comes right after them. Add aber for a change of feeling: Am Anfang war ich nervös, aber am Ende war ich glücklich.
cards.lead: You know the plan. Now you add two connectors from this chapter. Anna's model paragraph shows how they fit into a report.

examples.de: Die Anreise war lang. Trotzdem waren wir pünktlich.
examples.en: The journey there was long. Still, we were on time.
examples.why: Trotzdem: a surprising result.

examples.de: Es war sehr heiß, deshalb haben wir viel Wasser getrunken.
examples.en: It was very hot, so we drank a lot of water.
examples.why: Deshalb: a result you expect.

examples.de: Am Anfang war ich nervös, aber am Ende war ich glücklich.
examples.en: At the start I was nervous, but in the end I was happy.
examples.why: aber: position 0, subject first.

deeper.text: Choose the connector by the meaning. If the second sentence is the expected result, take deshalb: heiß, deshalb Wasser. If it is the surprise, take trotzdem: lang, trotzdem pünktlich. One of each in a short report is plenty. Too many make the text heavy. Keep the Perfekt for events.

example.de: Es hat geregnet. Trotzdem sind wir gelaufen.
example.en: It rained. Still, we ran.

cards.more: Result or surprise? Heat makes you thirsty: that is a normal result, so deshalb. Rain should keep you at home, but you run anyway: that is a surprise, so trotzdem. Both words sit at the start of the sentence, and the verb follows right behind them. Aber is different: it stands outside, and the subject comes next. Ask yourself before you write: would a friend be surprised? Yes: trotzdem. No: deshalb.

rows: Es war heiß, deshalb haben wir viel getrunken.
Die Anreise war lang. Trotzdem waren wir pünktlich.
Am Anfang war ich nervös, aber am Ende war ich glücklich.

steps: A normal result: deshalb
A surprise: trotzdem
A change of feeling: aber

cards.title: Culture: die Halle am Kanal
cards.body: The Halle am Kanal is a place made up for this course. It is an old factory (die Fabrik) by the canal (der Kanal). Today it has die Kletterhalle, die Sporthalle for der Verein „SV Kanalufer“ and the boats of a rowing club. Frau Weber was a good Ruderin when she was young.
cards.lead: A trip to a race often ends at a place of its own. Here is a place for sport that fits this chapter. You read about it in simple sentences.

examples.de: Die Halle am Kanal war früher eine Fabrik.
examples.en: The hall by the canal was a factory in the past.

examples.de: Heute gibt es dort eine Kletterhalle.
examples.en: Today there is a climbing hall there.

examples.de: Frau Weber war früher eine gute Ruderin.
examples.en: Frau Weber was a good rower in the past.

deeper.text: In der Kletterhalle you find die Kletterwand and das Seil. On the canal there are Boote, and people can rudern. Früher means in the past and goes with war: Die Halle war früher eine Fabrik. Old factory halls are often reused today, because they have a lot of space, high ceilings and a good location by the water.

example.de: Man kann auf dem Kanal rudern.
example.en: You can row on the canal.

cards.more: Imagine an old factory with big halls and a canal beside it. Nobody makes things there any more. Now people climb, play and row. It is the same building, but with a new life. The name tells the story: the hall at the canal. Walk through it in your mind: climbing wall and rope on the left, the sports hall for the club in the middle, the boats on the water at the back.
steps: Früher: a factory by the canal
Heute: a sports place
Three things to do: climb, play, row

cards.title: Culture: Sportvereine in D-A-CH
cards.body: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland many people are members of a sports club (der Sportverein). A club has teams (die Mannschaften) for children and adults. Many towns have a city run (der Stadtlauf). Popular sports are Fußball, Handball, Volleyball, Schwimmen, Radfahren and Laufen. You find clubs near you online.
cards.lead: The Halle am Kanal is invented, but clubs are real life. A few facts about sports clubs in German-speaking countries help you for your own report.

examples.de: In Deutschland sind viele Menschen Mitglied in einem Sportverein.
examples.en: In Germany many people are members of a sports club.

examples.de: Ein Verein hat Mannschaften für Kinder, Frauen und Männer.
examples.en: A club has teams for children, women and men.

examples.de: Auch in Österreich und in der Schweiz gibt es Stadtläufe.
examples.en: In Austria and in Switzerland there are also city runs.

deeper.text: A club is often a mix of training, friends and competitions. Members pay a small fee and can take part in the training. Many clubs have teams for young people. These are general facts, and every club is a bit different. Look at the club website to see what it offers.

example.de: Mira ist Mitglied im Verein „SV Kanalufer“.
example.en: Mira is a member of the club „SV Kanalufer“.

cards.more: A Sportverein is a bit like a family for one sport. You train with the same people every week. In summer you play outside, in winter you train in the hall, and sometimes you go to a Wettkampf together. In many towns there is a club for almost every sport, and children often start there. You pay a small fee, and in return you get a coach, a place and friends.

cards.title: Write your report in five steps
cards.body: Write your own report in five steps. 1 Plan: wohin, wann, mit wem. 2 Einleitung. 3 Three events in order with zuerst, dann, danach. 4 One deshalb and one trotzdem. 5 Schluss with a hope: Hoffentlich … Close with Viele Grüße and your name, without a comma.
cards.lead: You now have the words, the structure, the connectors and a place for the culture. Time to put it all into your own report, step by step.

examples.en: Hopefully I will come again soon.
It was worth it!
examples.why: A fixed chunk: use it as a whole.

examples.en: I will definitely come again.

deeper.text: Check your report like a list. Is there a title? Is the Einleitung short? Are there three events in the right order, each with a time word in position 1 and the verb right after it? Did you use deshalb and trotzdem once each? Does the Schluss say how you feel? Then you are ready.

example.de: Zuerst sind wir angekommen.
example.en: First we arrived.

cards.more: Think of the report as a ladder. Each step is one small job. Do not jump to the top. First the plan, then the start, then three events, then the contrast, then the end. After each step you already have a part of the text. At the end you add a feeling: Es hat sich gelohnt! means it was worth it, and Ich komme bestimmt wieder means I will definitely come again. Then only your name is missing.

rows: Ich bin mit Mira und Ben nach Hamburg gefahren.
Zuerst sind wir mit dem Zug gefahren. Danach haben wir in der Jugendherberge geschlafen.
Es hat sich gelohnt! Ich komme bestimmt wieder.

steps: 1 Plan: wohin, wann, mit wem
2 Einleitung: one or two sentences
3 Hauptteil: three events in order (zuerst, dann, danach)
4 One deshalb and one trotzdem
5 Schluss: your feeling and a hope, then Viele Grüße and your name (no comma)

reading.title: Liebe Grüße aus Hamburg!
reading.text:
Liebe Grüße aus Hamburg!

Liebe Leser,

ich bin zum ersten Mal in Hamburg und habe am Stadtlauf teilgenommen! Zuerst sind wir mit dem Zug gefahren. Die Anreise war lang, aber wir sind pünktlich angekommen. Wir haben in der Jugendherberge geschlafen. Am Morgen war ich sehr nervös. Trotzdem bin ich gelaufen. Ben hat mir seine Stoppuhr geliehen, und Mira hat mich angefeuert. Am Ende bin ich über die Ziellinie gelaufen. Die Atmosphäre war toll, und viele Fans haben gejubelt. Danach war die Siegerehrung. Ich war sehr müde, deshalb bin ich früh ins Bett gegangen. Aber ich bin glücklich. Es hat sich gelohnt!

Viele Grüße
Anna

listening.title: Hallo? … Was ist los?
listening.script:
Frau Weber: Hallo? Anna, sind Sie das? Was ist los? Sie klingen so traurig.
Anna: Hallo, Frau Weber. Ja, ich bin ein bisschen enttäuscht. Meine Zeit war nicht gut.
Frau Weber: Aber Sie haben doch am Stadtlauf teilgenommen! Das ist schon eine tolle Leistung.
Anna: Ich war so nervös, und ich habe schlecht geschlafen.
Frau Weber: Kopf hoch, Anna! Trotzdem sind Sie ins Ziel gekommen. Nächstes Mal klappt es bestimmt.
Anna: Vielen Dank, Frau Weber. Das ist nett.
Frau Weber: Wissen Sie, ich war früher eine gute Ruderin. Auch ich hatte einmal Pech bei einem Wettkampf. Trotzdem habe ich weitergemacht.
Anna: Ja, Sie haben recht.
Frau Weber: Kommen Sie morgen Abend ins Restaurant „Zum Löwen“! Herr Ali gibt den Läufern ein Getränk. Es ist gratis.
Anna: Wirklich? Das ist eine schöne Überraschung. Ich komme gern!
Frau Weber: Super! Bis morgen, Anna.
Anna: Bis morgen, Frau Weber.

free.prompt: Mein Reisebericht: write a short travel report (6 to 8 sentences) about a trip to a sports event or a match, real or invented. Write a short Einleitung (wohin, wann, mit wem), three events in order (zuerst, dann, danach, am Ende), one sentence with deshalb, one sentence with trotzdem and a Schluss with a hope. Close with Viele Grüße and your name on a new line, without a comma.
free.model:
Liebe Grüße aus Wien!

Am Samstag bin ich mit Freunden nach Wien gefahren. Wir haben ein Handballspiel gesehen. Zuerst sind wir mit dem Zug gefahren. Danach haben wir in einem Hotel geschlafen. Am Ende war das Spiel sehr spannend. Die Anreise war lang. Trotzdem waren wir pünktlich. Es war sehr laut, deshalb habe ich nicht gut gehört. Es hat sich gelohnt! Hoffentlich komme ich bald wieder.

Viele Grüße
Mira
